🤔 The eye reads the floor, but what about a wall? And we carry no distance sensor…

⏱️ Time: 5 minutes, then robots out

Recap by asking, not telling: “how does the robot know where it is?” Yesterday’s answers all live on the floor — the calibrated eye, the P follower, the two-eye square. Today’s problem stands upright: walls. We carry no distance sensor — and be accurate about why, because the easy answer is wrong. It is not that the ports ran out: port A is free on our robot (the stock kit is the thing with all six full). It is that a distance sensor would buy us nothing the wheels cannot already feel, and a stall is repeatable to the millimetre while an ultrasonic reading is not — so the spare port is better spent on a second eye, or on nothing. The cap that does bind us is the 4-motor limit (§5.2.8), and it binds mechanisms, not sensors: F and B drive, E and C grip, and that is the four. That constraint is the day’s gift — the drive motors themselves become touch sensors. Arc of the day: feel the wall (stall), back off a measured distance, wrap it in a patrol loop (yesterday’s if now lives inside a while), then bottle drive_to_wall + wall_square into the library and read the 255 scoresheet the anchor-first way. Keep this slide to five minutes: per the W2 delivery rhythm (decision #22), robots are out by minute 15, so the recap is a springboard, not a lecture.

Fix it: stall = touch, then back off 🧱
APPROACH_SPEED = 150         # deg/s, gentle, not a crash
right.run(APPROACH_SPEED)    # right rolls along…
left.run_until_stalled(APPROACH_SPEED,
                       duty_limit=50)   # …until LEFT jams
right.stop()
hub.speaker.beep()           # "I arrived"
drive_straight(-BACKOFF_MM)         # measured, repeatable
🤖 Robots out. Build it and tune BACKOFF_MM against the board. This is today’s competition in seven lines.


Gentle touch · wait for the jam · back off a measured BACKOFF_MM.



Stress the gentleness knobs: a low approach speed (≈150 deg/s) and duty_limit=50 — the duty limit caps how hard the motor is allowed to push, so the reading is crisp and the LEGO survives. Driving straight into a wall jams both wheels, so watching ONE motor is enough — run_until_stalled blocks on the left while the right just rolls. Line 6 calls their own drive_straight with a negative distance — the challenge parked at the library day is now urgent: flip the while comparison (or mirror it for negatives) in movements.py, two-minute fix, big payoff. Back-off is measured, not guessed — BACKOFF_MM = 50 ends exactly 5 cm off the wall, every run. (The pro equivalent, DriveBase.stalled(), arrives with the D8 reveal.)

Break it: the one-shot miss 😴

Your sense→act runs once. What happens at the second wall?

🤖 Robots out. Run it, aim it at a second wall by hand. Nothing.


Your code was right. It just stopped too soon, and that’s a loop’s job.



Let them run the one-shot to death on the real robot: it handles wall 1 perfectly, then dies — perfection that only lasts one event. The point is emotional before it’s technical: “your code was right — it just stopped too soon.” Loops are not a new trick from scratch; they already met while and for on Day 3’s square. Today those loops wrap a sensed decision instead of a fixed count of sides. (The animated one-shot-vs-patrol comparison lives in the 🏠 appendix.)

title: Stop at the Wall
text:
Name it: the patrol loop 🔁
hub.imu.reset_heading(0)
for lap in range(PATROL_LAPS):          # counted repeat = laps
    left.run(PATROL_SPEED); right.run(PATROL_SPEED)
    while not left.stalled():           # repeat until the wall
        if left_eye.reflection() < REFLECT_THRESHOLD:
            hub.speaker.beep(880)       # react, don't stop
        wait(10)
    left.stop(); right.stop()
    drive_straight(-BACKOFF_MM)                # measured back-off
    turn(90 * (lap + 1), absolute=True)   # absolute appointment


Two loops nested: for counts laps, while waits for the wall, and the if reacts on the move.



Read the shape aloud: outer for = “do this lap N times,” inner while not left.stalled() = “keep rolling until you feel the wall,” inner if = “and if you cross a staff line on the way, sing out” — yesterday’s calibrated threshold, reused as-is. The if living inside the while is the subtle win — reaction happens continuously during motion, not as a stop-and-check. (That’s also why this loop uses left.stalled() rather than the blocking run_until_stalled from this morning — the robot needs to keep checking things while it rolls.) turn(90 * (lap + 1), absolute=True) is the library day’s absolute-appointment trick doing its job silently: corner 1 aims at 90, corner 2 at 180 — a bumped corner can’t poison the next one. This program is the literal answer key for Gentle Giant’s loop bonus. With one board and no table borders yet, patrol two “walls” by moving the board between reps or using a wall + heavy box pair — the loop doesn’t care.

section: drive_to_wall and wall_square join the library 📦
text:
drive_to_wall and wall_square join the library 📦
def drive_to_wall(speed=150):
    """Roll gently until the wheels feel the wall."""
    right.run(speed)
    left.run_until_stalled(speed, duty_limit=50)
    right.stop()

def wall_square(heading=0):
    """Press BOTH wheels flat on the wall → truth restored."""
    left.run(120); right.run(120)
    while not (left.stalled() and right.stalled()):
        wait(10)
    left.stop(); right.stop()
    hub.imu.reset_heading(heading)   # the wall never lies
    drive_straight(-BACKOFF_MM)


Both wheels flat on the wall → heading known again. The wall never lies.



Same promotion ritual as the library day: the morning’s loose fix-it lines get names and move into movements.py, right under drive_straight and turn. Walk wall_square slowly — it’s the first verb whose output is trust, not motion: waiting for BOTH motors to stall means the bumper is flat on the wall, so the physical world just told you your heading exactly; reset_heading(heading) writes that truth back into the gyro, and the measured back-off leaves you at a known distance too. Gyro drift accumulates over a 2-minute run — squaring is how Weeks 3–4 missions reset it between tasks, which is why this humble verb outlives almost everything else. Demo: spin the robot a few times by hand (drift injected), wall_square, then a turn(90, absolute=True) — still true. Table note (decision #23): until the bordered table exists, wall_square trains on the fixed board; when the table lands we re-validate it at the true border positions — that’s the table-arrival checkpoint.

title: The Drive That Heals Itself
text:
The fix, in code
def gyro_turn(target):                        # def = name a move once, use it forever
    hub.imu.reset_heading(0)
    left.run(200); right.run(-200)            # fast for the long haul…
    while hub.imu.heading() < target - 30:
        wait(5)
    left.run(50); right.run(-50)              # …crawl the last 30°
    while hub.imu.heading() < target:
        wait(5)
    left.stop(); right.stop()

gyro_turn(90)     # or gyro_turn(45), gyro_turn(180)…


Two speeds, two whiles: fast for the long haul, crawl the last 30°, so momentum arrives with nothing left to steal. And line 1: def names the move once, and every call replays it.



First def of the bootcamp — land it hard: a function is a named move, exactly like run_angle is someone else’s named move. This version handles right turns (positive targets); if a kid asks about left turns, brilliant — flip the two run signs and the < to >, or park it as a challenge. The constants 200/50/30 are the raw material the afternoon interrogates; they get promoted into the ROBOT FACTS block at D8. Demo on the next slide — walk the highlights here first.

text:
🐛 Bug hunt: the silent robot

No red error. No crash. The robot just… sits there. The code looks perfect. What did we forget?

def gyro_turn(target):
    hub.imu.reset_heading(0)
    left.run(200); right.run(-200)
    while hub.imu.heading() < target:
        wait(5)
    left.stop(); right.stop()


def only writes the recipe, it never cooks it. Nothing happens until you call the move by name: add gyro_turn(90) below. Defining a move and using a move are two separate steps.



The most instructive bug of the week — no error to read, so the robot’s stillness is the message. Elicit first: “if the code is right, why no movement?” Draw the split on the board — def …: writes the recipe card, gyro_turn(90) hands it to the cook. Leads straight into the bench lab, where they call it three times.

🐢 Sleepy check: the crawl always covers the last 30°. Which call spends the biggest slice of its turn crawling, and what does that do to its time?
🚀 Fly-past check: you crank the fast speed to beat the clock. Which call now risks blowing past its tick, and why that one?

title: The Drive That Heals Itself
text:
You already run this controller 🚶






The game


Stand three big steps from the wall. Walk to it and stop with your toes exactly on the line. Round 1: normal. Round 2: robot style, full speed then slam the brakes at the end. Round 3: crawl the entire way. Which round felt right, and what were your legs doing in it?





Your legs already run the deal: far → fast · close → gentle · there → zero. No zones, no steps. Your speed simply follows the distance left, and robots can sign the same deal.


⏱️ Time: 5 minutes

Same unplugged-first habit as the D3 inner-ear game. Round 2 reproduces the coast (they’ll lean past the line or stutter-brake); round 3 is the sleepy 45. Ask round-1 walkers to narrate their own speed out loud — “fast… slower… slower… stop” — that sentence is the controller.

title: The Drive That Heals Itself
text:
Say the deal in numbers

Target 90°, heading reads 20°. Call the degrees-left the error, which is 70 here. Build the wheel speed from the error: you’re allowed one multiplication.
What does your rule give at error 70? At 10? At 0?



  speed = error × KP  (KP = 4)
  error 70 → speed 280  flat out 🚀
  error 10 → speed 40    tiptoe 🐢
  error 0  → speed 0     parks itself 🎯




speed = error × KP: the whole staircase in one line. KP is the slope, and engineers call this knob the gain: how hard to push per degree left. At error 0 the speed is 0, so it parks itself.



Elicit the multiplication — don’t reveal it. Most squads propose “speed = distance left” first; ask “what if the wheels need bigger numbers?” and the × KP falls out — name it once out loud (“its code name is KP; engineers call it the gain”) and use KP from here on. The three sample rows are the wall-walk in numbers: narrate them as “fast… slower… stop”, same sentence as the game.

title: The Drive That Heals Itself
text:
The proportional turn
def gyro_turn_p(target, kp=4):
    hub.imu.reset_heading(0)
    while abs(target - hub.imu.heading()) > 1:   # until within 1°…
        error = target - hub.imu.heading()       # degrees still to go
        left.run(kp * error)                     # far → fast
        right.run(-kp * error)                   # close → gentle
        wait(5)
    left.stop(); right.stop()

gyro_turn_p(90)   # gyro_turn_p(45)… gyro_turn_p(180)… gyro_turn_p(-90)!


Line 10: a negative target flips the sign and the wheels swap, so left turns come free. Yesterday’s version needed surgery for that.



Walk the highlight stops: kp arrives as a parameter with a default — new syntax, teach it in one breath (“a knob you can leave alone”). Line 3’s abs() is what makes negative targets work. Demo on the next slide.
Coach aside — “why run() and not motor.dc()?” (for the sharp student who’s read ahead). Honest truth: run() is itself a closed-loop speed controller inside Pybricks — so this hand-written P sits on top of it, a controller-on-a-controller. Your kp sets a speed target; Pybricks’ own loop chases it. A pro writing a controller from scratch often reaches for motor.dc() instead — raw power/duty — so their formula is the whole controller, one layer, nothing hidden underneath. Totally legitimate, and purer. We keep run() on purpose for two reasons: it’s smoother and battery-proof (a fresh vs. tired hub turns the same — priceless with five robots on the bench), and it speaks the same “speed” language as robot.drive(speed, turn) and DriveBase — so speed = error × KP stays literally true all the way from this turn, through the self-healing straight, to D6’s line-follower. dc() is the right tool the day you build a controller with no help underneath; that day isn’t this bootcamp.

Name it: D damps 🛑
def gyro_turn_pd(target, kp=4, kd=0.5):
    hub.imu.reset_heading(0)
    last_error = target
    while abs(target - hub.imu.heading()) > 1:
        error = target - hub.imu.heading()    # how FAR (P)
        change = (error - last_error) / 0.005 # how FAST (D, in °/s)
        last_error = error
        left.run(kp * error + kd * change)    # ease off early
        right.run(-(kp * error + kd * change))
        wait(5)
    left.stop(); right.stop()





P (Proportional)


Reads where you are
Pushes hard when far
Engine of the turn





D (Derivative)


Reads how fast gap closes
Taps the brake before arrival
Stops ringing and overshoot 🛑





Focus on the three new lines: remember last error, subtract to get rate of change, and combine into the motor command. When closing fast on the target, error shrinks each loop pass, making change negative. Multiplying by kd subtracts power, giving a smooth deceleration right into 90°.

def drive_straight(distance_mm, speed=400):
    """Drive distance_mm while holding gyro heading."""
    heading = hub.imu.heading()                    # lock current heading
    finish = left.angle() + distance_mm * DEG_PER_MM
    while left.angle() < finish:                   # encoder finish line
        error = hub.imu.heading() - heading        # gyro correction
        left.run(speed - KP * error)
        right.run(speed + KP * error)
        wait(5)
    left.stop(); right.stop()

The gyro P-loop holds the heading straight

Local variables


Created inside a function
Gone the moment the function returns

Global constants


Defined at the top of the file
Visible across all functions
Update once to tune the entire robot

turn(…, absolute=True) lands within ±2° of target heading (10 runs)

Can explain what D and I add to P

title: Gears
text:
Feel it: the heavy lift 🏋️

Clamp something heavy, like a full water bottle. Lift.
What happens? Why? The motor is trying its hardest, so where is the strength going?



The motor isn’t weak. The ratio is. Your gears hand the claw exactly the strength the motor makes, 1 : 1.



The engineered failure that makes gear theory land as a rescue instead of a lecture. With the 1:1 bevel pairs, a genuinely heavy object slips or stalls the medium motor — let them feel it strain, and don’t let a stall cook the motor for more than a moment. Then the hook question: “a car engine can’t lift a car either — yet the jack in the trunk lifts it with one hand. What’s the trick?” Someone will say gears or leverage — that someone just introduced Act B for you.

title: Gears
section: Break it: two claws, one brain 🧠
text:
Break it: two claws, one brain 🧠

Carry the bottle in the top claw. Now open the bottom claw without moving the top one.
Try. What happens? Is this a feature or a bug?



Both. One motor → two claws is a motor saved, and 4 motors is the Elementary cap (§5.2.8). The price is that they always move together. Engineering is knowing the price. 🏷️



The coupling discovery, on their own design decision. Name the budget correctly, because this is where it is usually got wrong: our robot has a spare port (A); what it does not have is a spare motor — F and B drive, E and C grip, and Elementary allows 4, maximum (§5.2.8). A second gripper motor is what we cannot afford, not a second plug.
Praise the trade before naming its cost, then plant the question that decides whether the price is affordable: does any moment in the anchor run need “top claw holding” AND “bottom claw moving” at once? Have squads check against the cables → mic sequence. If yes, the fixes are geometry (each claw engages in a different part of the rotation range) or making one claw passive — a design conversation for the build block. Point at the build itself: have a squad trace motor shaft → axle → gear pair → claw arm with a finger, and the coupling is right there in their hands.

title: Gears
text:
Count teeth, know the future

Every gear question starts the same way: count the teeth.
Ratio = follower teeth ÷ driver teeth.



  
  
  
  
  
  in: 1 turn
  
  
  
  out: 1 turn
  
  
  
  20T
  20T
  bevel pair: 90° corner
  
  follower ÷ driver
  20 ÷ 20 = 1 : 1
  same speed · same strength
  all it buys: the 90° corner




Bevel gears buy direction, not strength. Your gripper spent its gears on the corner, so the lift failed.




Teeth = size: meshing gears share tooth size. It’s a ratio, so unlike the wheel, π cancels. Just count. 🔢



Keep the arithmetic tiny: teeth in, teeth out, one division. Have every squad physically count the teeth on a spare bevel gear — counting beats being told. The reveal sentence is the punchline of Act A: their gear pair spends its entire budget on turning the axis 90° (which the build needs — motor lies flat, claws swing on vertical axles) and has nothing left for strength. Now the fix is obvious before it’s taught: change the ratio.

title: Gears
text:
The trade: speed ⇄ strength

  
    driver 24T → follower:
    12T
    24T
    36T
  
  
    DRIVER 24T
    FOLLOWER
    
      
      
      
      
      
    
    
      
      
      
      
      
    
  
  




Small drives big → slower but stronger. Speed and strength are one budget, and gears decide how to spend it.


Click through the three followers and narrate the yellow spokes — the driver is always the 24T, only the follower changes. 12T: the claw spins twice as fast and grips half as hard. 24T: exactly the motor, no bonus — the same 1:1 deal their own bevel pair gives them. 36T: gives up a third of its speed and buys half again the strength (×1.5). One sentence carries the slide: “speed and strength are the same budget — gears just move money between the accounts.”
Then link each direction to a mission verb: gear for torque where a push needs force (cable pusher against friction), for speed where it needs reach (a claw that must open wide in a hurry). Physical demo beats the animation if time allows: hold a 12T driving a 36T between two fingers and feel the follower resist. Resist the full gear zoo — idlers, racks, worms and compound trains are continuation-season material. title: Gears
text:
Challenge: tune YOUR gripper 🛠️






Pick one, 20 minutes



💪 Stronger: re-gear so the bottle lift succeeds, and prove it with the lift
⚡ Faster: re-gear so open→close beats the stopwatch, and prove it with a timed cycle





Rules: same motor, same port, only the gears change
Still fits the 250 mm cube with claws closed 📏
Before you build: say the ratio out loud. Predict, then prove


Modification is their proven skill — this stretches it one step, with a prediction gate (“say the ratio before you touch a gear”) so the theory does the work. Squads choose their own goal; both choices are correct, which quietly teaches that gearing is a decision, not an answer. Watch for the classic trap: gearing so slow the claw takes 5 seconds to close — a run costs time. If a squad finishes early: “now make the two claws close at different speeds from the same motor” — a compound ratio discovered, not assigned. This is also where mechanism talent becomes visible post-draft; watch who leads the rebuild.

Where we left off



Yesterday
The trick




📏 Distance
count degrees: 1 turn = 27.6 cm


🧭 Blindfolded
no checking → it drifts




🤔 It knows how far its wheels spun. But which way is it pointing?

⏱️ Time: 10 minutes

title: Drive a Square
text:
Setup, same as yesterday
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor
from pybricks.parameters import Port, Direction
from pybricks.tools import wait

hub = PrimeHub()
left = Motor(Port.F, Direction.COUNTERCLOCKWISE)   # yours
right = Motor(Port.B)                              # yours

Everyone types this once at the top and keeps it for the whole day. Raw motors only, on purpose — through D7 the students build the whole driver and library by hand; the polished shortcut (DriveBase) waits until the D8 reveal (decision #20, re-timed by #26), a reward earned piece by piece.

title: Drive a Square
text:
One corner = how many degrees? 🤔

A side is easy: 30 cm → 391°. But when the robot spins in place, how far does each wheel roll?
Watch the wheels from above. What shape do they draw?


Sketch it. Write down a wheel-degrees guess. 👀


Pure prediction — do NOT derive or reveal anything here. Collect shape guesses (a line? a spiral? a circle?) and a wheel-degrees number from every squad on the board; wrong guesses make the next slide land harder. The derivation happens after the demo’s traces give the shape away. Do NOT mention slip or scrub anywhere in this act — the math is honest, and the square is about to betray it anyway. That betrayal lands harder if they trust the number when it arrives.

title: Drive a Square
text:
The wheels answer: the turn-circle 🛞

  
    
    
    
    
      
      
      
      
      
    
    
  
  
    
      robot turned: 0°
      tire rolled: 0.0 cm → 0°
    
    
      rope around the circle = 3.14 × 12.8 ≈ 40.2 cm
      one corner = rope ÷ 4 ≈ 10.0 cm of rolling
      × 13.04 (yesterday's translator) → TURN_ANGLE ≈ 131°
    
    
      ▶ Turn 90°
      ▶ Turn 180°
      ↺ reset
    
    
      tire gap: 12.8 cm
      
    
  




That gap has a name: the axle track, the wheel-to-wheel distance, ≈ 12.8 cm on the coach’s base. Wider robot → longer rope → bigger corner. Measure your own. Nobody copies 131.



This is the reveal for the last slide’s question — click BEFORE explaining. Hit Turn 90° with their guesses on the board: both tires drag a quarter of the dashed circle, the shape question answers itself on screen, and the ¼ rope ≈ 10.0 cm label lands right on the arc they just watched. Now the three formula lines, one fragment at a time, each reading its number off the picture: rope around the circle (3.14 × gap) — say it as yesterday’s move: “rope around the rim gave you 27.6; same trick, bigger circle, drawn on the mat” — then a quarter of it (the labeled arc), × 13.04 → 131, next to their guesses. Don’t re-teach the translator — 13.04 is yesterday’s number; a quick “who remembers what 13.04 does?” is enough. Click three more times: a full robot-turn = the whole circle’s rope. Save the Turn 180° button for the about-face slide two slides ahead — it shows ½ rope live and confirms ≈262. Then the payoff: drag the tire gap slider wider — every line updates live and TURN_ANGLE grows. Wider robot = more rolling per corner — that’s why every squad measures their own gap (≈128 mm on our build; the stock ADB is ≈114 mm). Teal trace = right tire, coral = left, same colors as the code comments.

title: Drive a Square
text:
Unroll the formula 🧵
Your 131 is right. But every number is one of yesterday’s ropes. Unroll them and watch π vanish:

  TURN_ANGLE = 3.14 × 12.8 ÷ 4  × 13.04
             = 3.14 × 12.8 ÷ 4  × 360 ÷ (3.14 × 8.8)
             = 3.14 × 12.8 × 90 ÷ (3.14 × 8.8)
             = 90 × 12.8 ÷ 8.8 ≈ 131°



TURN_ANGLE = turn × gap ÷ wheel. The two 3.14s cancel. Keep gap and wheel in your pocket… 😏



Act 3 of the turn-circle story: question → wheels answer → unroll the answer. Elicit the substitution, don’t re-teach it — both ropes are Day-2 property: “what IS 13.04?” (360 ÷ 27.6) and “what was 27.6?” (3.14 × 8.8, the wheel’s rope). The only NEW thing on this slide is the cancellation: same 3.14 on top and bottom → cancels; 360 ÷ 4 → 90. What’s left is 90 × gap ÷ wheel: sanity-check on the calculator, 90 × 12.8 ÷ 8.8 = 130.9 ≈ their 131. The pocket line is a deliberate plant: gap and wheel diameter are exactly the two numbers DriveBase asks for at the D8 reveal — when that deck asks “why does it need the axle track?”, call back to this cancellation. Land at least the final gap ÷ wheel line with everyone; if a squad is drowning in the algebra, the demo intuition carries the load — skim the middle steps and move on.

title: Drive a Square
section: Prove you own it: the about-face 🔄
text:
Prove you own it: the about-face 🔄

Judge wants a full 180° about-face. In turn × gap ÷ wheel, which number changes?
Say it first, then calculate.



  corner:     90 × 12.8 ÷ 8.8 ≈ 131°
  about-face: 180 × 12.8 ÷ 8.8 ≈ 262°




Only the turn changed, from 90 to 180, so the answer roughly doubles. Gap and wheel are your robot’s fingerprint. The turn is your order.



This is the payoff of the unroll: the formula generalizes. Elicit before revealing — most squads will say “the 90 becomes 180”; make them commit, then show the line. If anyone doubts it, flip back two slides and hit Turn 180° on the turn-circle demo: the label shows ½ rope ≈ 20.1 cm and the tire counter lands on ≈262 — the picture and the formula agree. Fast squads: ask for the octagon corner (45° → 45 × 12.8 ÷ 8.8 ≈ 65°) — they’ll need it after the loop slide. Every squad substitutes their own measured gap, not 12.8.

text:
The square, by hand
SIDE_ANGLE = 391    # 30 cm × 13.04, yesterday's translator
TURN_ANGLE = 131    # YOUR number: ¼ turn-circle, translated
SPEED = 400         # deg/s

left.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE, wait=False)    # side 1
right.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE)
left.run_angle(SPEED, TURN_ANGLE, wait=False)    # corner 1: wheels roll opposite ways…
right.run_angle(SPEED, -TURN_ANGLE)              # …so the robot spins in place

# your turn: copy-paste until you have 4 sides + 4 corners
Run it. A square! …ish. Hold your corner questions. First, a code smell. 👃

Let them build it the obvious way: select the four motor lines, copy, paste ×3. It runs, and something square-ish appears — do NOT investigate the corners yet; that’s the next act. This slide is about the program: ~16 near-identical lines. Watch for squads that miss a paste or drop a minus sign — those bugs are teaching gold for the quiz that follows.

title: Drive a Square
text:
Quick quiz 🚨

Your square = ~16 copy-pasted lines. Now the judge wants an octagon. Then a triangle. How many lines each time?
Would you bet a competition run on 32 pasted lines?



32 pasted lines, one flipped minus sign away from a broken corner. Repeating yourself breeds bugs. Repeats are the computer’s job.

title: Drive a Square
text:
The rescue: repeat with for
for side in range(4):            # do the indented lines 4 times
    print("side number", side)

Run it: prints 0, 1, 2, 3. Computers start counting at 0.
Everything indented under the for is inside the loop.



range(4) = “4 times.” Write it once, repeat it. A square = one corner, four times.

title: Drive a Square
text:
🐛 Bug hunt: the missing colon

This for loop won’t even start. Pybricks flags the first line in red. What’s missing?

for side in range(4)
    left.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE, wait=False)
    right.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE)


SyntaxError: no colon. Every repeat header ends in :, which says “block starts here.” Fix: for side in range(4):



The colon is invisible until it’s missing — run it live so the red SyntaxError lands on the for line. Make the habit loud: say “colon” out loud every time you type a for or while header this week. This is the #1 typo of the day; naming it now saves ten rescues later.

title: Drive a Square
text:
🐛 Bug hunt: the runaway line

The colon’s there now… and it still won’t run. Read the error. It points at line 2.

for side in range(4):
left.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE, wait=False)
right.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE)


IndentationError: lines inside a loop must be pushed in (one Tab). No indent, no “inside.” The spaces tell Python what repeats.



Indentation-as-meaning is the single biggest beginner hurdle — spend a beat. Show both side by side: flush-left (crashes) vs. indented (runs). Then the sneaky version if time allows: indent only line 2 — no crash, but the right wheel fires once, outside the loop. “It ran but it’s wrong” is scarier than a crash, and that’s exactly the lesson.

title: Drive a Square
section: The square: one corner, four times
text:
The square: one corner, four times
SIDE_ANGLE = 391    # same constants as before…
TURN_ANGLE = 131
SPEED = 400

for side in range(4):
    left.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE, wait=False)    # counted → sides are solid
    right.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE)
    left.run_angle(SPEED, TURN_ANGLE, wait=False)    # wheels roll opposite ways…
    right.run_angle(SPEED, -TURN_ANGLE)              # …so the robot spins in place
~16 lines → 8. Octagon? range(8) plus one new corner number: two edits.
Now mark your start with tape. Run it three times. Where does it finish?

Close the octagon promise fast: range(8) plus a 45° corner — 45 × 12.8 ÷ 8.8 ≈ 65° — two edits, and a fast squad can try it. Sides use run_angle — yesterday’s tool — so the four sides come out even and repeatable. That’s deliberate: it isolates the failure to the turns. And the 131 is their honest math from this morning, so nobody can blame the number — tires scrub and slip in a pivot, so 131 wheel-degrees ≠ 90 robot-degrees, and it varies run to run. Let them run 3× and watch the last corner miss the tape by a different amount each time.

title: Drive a Square
text:
The square that never closes



The wheels really did roll 131°. Your math was right.
But a spinning tire slips → a different angle every run. Counting fixes distance, never heading.
Your robot needs a sense of direction.


⏱️ Time: 25 minutes

title: Drive a Square
text:
You already own this sensor 🧍






The game


Stand up, arms out, eyes closed. Your partner slowly turns you a random amount, maybe a quarter turn, maybe more. Eyes still closed: point at the door.




Most of you will point close. How?! You saw nothing. No wheels counted anything.



Your inner ear feels turning. Robots have it too: the gyro, awake inside the hub this whole time.


⏱️ Time: 5 minutes

title: Drive a Square
text:
One number for “which way”: heading

  
    
    
    
    
    
    0°
    90°
    180°
    -90°
    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
    
  
  
    
      hub.imu.heading()→ 0°
    
    
      ⟲ Twist left 45°
      ⟳ Twist right 45°
      reset_heading(0)
    
  




heading = degrees turned from where you started. Right = up, left = down. Keep spinning → 360, 450, 720…



Drive the demo from their answers: “if I twist it right a quarter turn, what will the number say?” Click, confirm. “Left half a turn from there?” Click. Then the trap: twist right 8× — the number passes 360 and keeps going. Heading is total turning, not a clock face. reset_heading(0) is the “THIS way is zero” button — they’ll use it in every program today.

title: Drive a Square
text:
What the robot sees


Bridge from the toy demo to the real thing: this readout is real — hub.imu.heading() is one line of code, and 0° is simply wherever the robot pointed when you zeroed it. The next slide puts this exact printout on their own hubs.

title: Drive a Square
text:
Lab: feel the gyro 🖐️
hub.imu.reset_heading(0)        # "THIS way is zero"

for _ in range(100):            # ~10 seconds of just… feeling
    print(hub.imu.heading())
    wait(100)

Pick the robot up. Twist it left, right, all the way around. The numbers follow your hands. No motor moved.
Spin one slow full circle → 360. Keep going → 720!

⏱️ Time: 10 minutes

title: Drive a Square
text:
Quick quiz 🚨

Twist the robot right 90°… then left 90°. What does heading() read now?
90? 180? 0? Something else? Vote first, then try it.



0. Heading is net turning: +90 − 90 = 0. A compass needle, not a step counter.

title: Drive a Square
text:
Plan it in words first

You can left.run(200), left.stop(), and read hub.imu.heading() live. In plain words, how do you turn exactly 90°?
No code. Say the plan out loud.



“Spin. Keep watching the heading. The instant it says 90, stop.” A turn that watches itself. New trick: repeating while something is true.

title: Drive a Square
text:
New trick: while
while hub.imu.heading() < 90:   # as long as this check is TRUE…
    wait(5)                     # …wait 5 ms, then check again

for repeats a known count. while repeats while a check is true.
This loop does nothing but watch, hundreds of gyro checks per second.



The program parks on the while until the check turns false. “Stare until it’s time” is every robot’s heartbeat.

title: Drive a Square
section: The watched turn: your first gyro move
text:
The watched turn: your first gyro move
hub.imu.reset_heading(0)

left.run(200)                   # left wheel forward…
right.run(-200)                 # …right wheel backward = spin in place
while hub.imu.heading() < 90:   # watch the gyro…
    wait(5)
left.stop()                     # …and stop AT 90. Not "about" 90.
right.stop()
wait(1000)                      # let the coast settle before reading
print(hub.imu.heading())        # moment of truth 👀
Run it. What did it print?

Everyone runs it and reports their printed number. Nobody gets exactly 90 — expect 92–96 depending on speed and battery. Don’t explain yet; collect the numbers on the board and let the next slide interrogate them. The wait(1000) before the print is load-bearing, not filler: the robot keeps coasting for a beat after stop(), and reading heading() the instant you call it can catch that motion mid-flight and under-report the overshoot — the settle-wait is what makes the printed number (and the “it printed 94” quiz on the next slide) trustworthy.

title: Drive a Square
text:
Quiz: it printed 94. Who’s guilty? 🚨

The gyro lying? Python too slow? The robot broken?
Hint: try to freeze yourself mid-spin.



Momentum. stop() is instant, but a spinning robot isn’t. It coasts past the line, like a car braking. The gyro told the truth: you did end at 94.



Deliberate cliffhanger: the squad leaves with the thief named (momentum) but not yet arrested — the diagnosis is today’s property, the cure is D4’s opening act. If a squad proposes “just ask for 86”, park it with “would 86 survive a battery swap?” and move on; fudge factors are exactly what tomorrow’s fix makes unnecessary. If someone asks why this turn feels jerkier than yesterday’s run_angle glide, it’s the same culprit: no easing off + coast-on-stop() produces both the overshoot number and the lurch — run_angle decelerated into its target, which is why it felt smoother (and still drifted). Fuller version lands on the watched-square slide.

⏱️ Time: 20 minutes

title: Drive a Square
section: The watched square: a loop in a loop
text:
The watched square: a loop in a loop
SIDE_ANGLE = 391    # 30 cm, yesterday's translator
SPEED = 400

for side in range(4):
    left.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE, wait=False)   # side: counted degrees
    right.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE)
    hub.imu.reset_heading(0)                        # corner: watched, not guessed
    left.run(200); right.run(-200)
    while hub.imu.heading() < 90:
        wait(5)
    left.stop(); right.stop()

A while inside a for: the count loop draws, the watch loop lands each corner.
What’s gone: no 131. The gyro speaks robot-degrees. Ask 90, it watches 90.



Tape your start. Run 3× beside the blind square: closer, and off by the same few degrees each time. A bug you can predict is a bug you can fix. 😏




Watch the motion, though: yesterday’s counted square glided, and this one lurches to each stop. That’s not the gyro, it’s us flooring it and then cutting power. Smooth ≠ right: the smooth one drifted. Tomorrow: smooth and right. 😏



The day’s two loops, nested — say it out loud: for repeats a known count, while repeats while a check is true, and a real robot program is almost always one inside the other. The comparison is the point: the blind square missed by a different amount each run (scrub and slip), the watched square misses by the same ~4° coast every corner. Consistency is the gyro’s gift — it converts a random bug into a predictable one, which is exactly what D4 exploits.
Field the “but yesterday’s turn was smoother” objection with the purple card, don’t dodge it: run_angle eased off the gas into its target (smooth ride, but slip-blind — it drifted), while this while/stop() turn runs flat-out then coasts (honest heading, rough ride). If a squad says “the calculation looked nicer,” agree — then point at where each square finished: smooth lost on accuracy. The lurch is a driving problem D4 cures (arrive slowly, then a controller), not a gyro problem — do NOT preview the fix, just name that it’s coming.

title: Drive a Square
text:
Pro move: targets that climb 🧗

Each corner resets heading to 0. But heading keeps counting: 360, 450, 720… What if you never reset, and aim corner 1 at 90, corner 2 at 180, corner 3 at 270?
Where would the coast go?


hub.imu.reset_heading(0)                    # once, before the loop
for side in range(4):
    left.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE, wait=False)
    right.run_angle(SPEED, SIDE_ANGLE)
    left.run(200); right.run(-200)
    while hub.imu.heading() < 90 * (side + 1):   # 90, 180, 270, 360
        wait(5)
    left.stop(); right.stop()



The target is built from the loop variable, so the coast stops piling up: overshoot to 94, and corner 2 has 4° less to turn. Each mistake pays for the next. Fast squads: race both squares. Which closes tighter?



Stretch material — gate nobody on it. It’s the payoff of the earlier “keep spinning → 360, 450, 720” trap AND the first time an expression (90 * (side + 1)) does work inside a loop. The insight — absolute targets absorb per-corner error instead of accumulating it — is a real WRO technique they’ll meet again in mission code. If time is short, demo it coach-side in 2 minutes, then move on — the next slide (Any Shape) is the one that feeds Shape Shifter. Forward hook for coaches: this is the seed of the library’s turn(…, absolute=True), which drops the per-turn reset entirely when the library is written (Name Your Moves), and it comes back when headings get read straight off a map of the mat.

Any shape, two numbers 🔺⬣

      of turning
    
    
      sides = –
    
    
    
      Triangle

Every corner adds up to one full lap, 360°, so corner = 360 ÷ sides.

A new shape in the code is just two edits: the range(...) count and that corner angle.


Elicit the 360 with bodies first, not algebra: one student walks a triangle on the mat and ends facing the way they started — however many corners, the turning always totals one full spin. Then drive the demo from their guesses: pick Triangle, each corner flashes its 120° turn right on the shape while the dial climbs 120 → 240 → 360 and closes; pick Octagon, eight skinny 45s stack to the same 360. title: Drive a Square
text:
Shape Shifter 🔺⬛⬣






The challenge


The judge calls a shape, triangle up to octagon. 60 seconds to edit and run: range(?) plus corner = 360 ÷ sides. Score = gap from tape to finish, tiebreak = fewest lines touched. 3 calls, best two count.




Two edits per shape. That’s the whole race. Copy-pasters meet their doom at the octagon. 😈
Pro question: which drifts more, 3 fat corners or 8 skinny ones? Watch your traces and keep the answer for tomorrow.


Uses exactly today’s material: for + range, the watched-turn while, 360 ÷ n, and heading — no def; that arrives tomorrow. The 60-second edit window is the point: a loop makes a new shape a two-number change, so the octagon call separates loopers from pasters on the clock. The closure gap keeps the coast visible — 8 corners × ~4° beats 3 × ~4°, so the octagon drifts more; squads that see that are already leaning into tomorrow’s cure. Coach scorecard: edit discipline (two calm edits vs. a rewrite), 360 ÷ n reasoning without a calculator, and who re-tapes and re-tests between calls.

title: Drive a Square
text:
Today’s gate






You’re done today when…


The judge calls any shape → your loop draws it with watched corners (two edits, no copy-paste). You can explain heading, walk your watched turn line by line, and name who’s guilty for the 94.




Tomorrow: the coast meets its cure, which is to arrive slowly. Then the cure gets a brain: speed that shrinks with the error. One formula, and it has a name every roboticist knows.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
Yesterday’s two numbers


What you measured

One wheel turn rolls 27.6 cm
\(C = \pi \times d\), from unrolling the rope


What I handed you

\(360 \div 27.6 \approx 13.04°\) per cm
\(100 \times 13.04 \approx 1304°\)




Be honest: you followed that. You did not invent it. So what happens on the mat in Week 4 when the number isn’t 100 cm, but 42 cm, then 17, then 63? You need the tool, not the answer. 🧰

⏱️ Time: 5 minutes · no laptops yet

title: The Beam Balance
text:
Same symbol, two jobs


In Python ➡️
speed = 200
“Put 200 in the room called speed.”
An arrow. It does something.

On paper ⚖️
\[27.6 \times t = 30\]
“These two weigh the same.”
A balance. It states something.



Today is all about the paper one. Every time you see = on the whiteboard for the next hour, picture a beam with two pans, and picture it tipping the moment you cheat.



This distinction is the single most common source of confusion when beginners meet algebra alongside a first programming language, and this cohort is meeting both in the same week. Say it out loud, then keep pointing at it: the whiteboard = and the editor = are different animals wearing the same costume. Do not skip the callout — the arcade recap re-tests exactly this.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
The prop






What’s on the table


A balance (or a ruler resting on a pencil), and bricks as fruit:

🍊 orange = one 2×4 brick, our unit
🍌 banana = two bricks stuck together
🍉 melon = three bricks stuck together





Everything today is counted in oranges. A banana is worth 2. A melon is worth 3.
The students don’t know those numbers yet. They work them out from the beam.


Coach prep: if no pan balance is in the kit, a 30 cm ruler across a round pencil works, or draw the beam on the whiteboard and place bricks in two taped-off “pans” while you declare level/tipped. A physical tip is worth a lot here — the whole lesson runs on the memory of watching it fall. Do NOT reveal banana=2 and melon=3; those are the answers to sections D and F. Build the fruit ahead of time so bricks can’t be counted at a glance — tape over the studs if your group is sharp-eyed.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
6 oranges balance 6 apples

🍊🍊🍊🍊🍊🍊  ⚖️  🍏🍏🍏🍏🍏🍏
I take one orange off the left and one apple off the right. Hands up: does it tip, or stay level?



Level. Take the same away from both sides and the beam doesn’t care. That is what subtraction means on a balance. Do it four more times and you are down to 1 🍊 = 1 🍏.


⏱️ Time: 6 minutes

title: The Beam Balance
text:
Now the other direction

Put one orange back on the left and one apple back on the right → still level. That’s plus.
Put one orange on the left only → 💥 it tips. Everyone sees it.




The rule, first draft

Whatever you do to one side, do to the other side too.
Write it on the board. We are going to catch it lying in about four minutes. 🕵️



Deliberately let them write down the sloppy version. The rule as stated here is the one almost every textbook gives, and it is exactly wrong enough to break in section D. Break it → feel it → fix it applies to rules, not just code.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
New puzzle: 6 oranges balance 3 bananas

🍊🍊🍊🍊🍊🍊  ⚖️  🍌🍌🍌
Follow your own rule. Take one thing off each side. Still level?




💥 It tips. Hard.

Five oranges on the left. Two bananas on the right. Let them watch it fall before you say a word.


⏱️ Time: 10 minutes

title: The Beam Balance
section: So why did it work the first time?
text:
So why did it work the first time?

6 oranges balanced 6 apples. Same count on both sides…
…so one apple had to weigh exactly one orange. The beam told us that for free.
Removing 1 orange and 1 apple removed the same weight from each pan. ✅
But a banana is heavier than an orange. Removing one of each removed different weights. ❌




The rule, final version

Do the same amount to both sides, not the same number of objects.



This is the highest-value slide in the deck. The object-vs-amount confusion is the exact failure that shows up years later as “I cancelled the x from both sides.” Land it now, cheaply, with bricks. If a student objects that they can’t know a banana weighs 2 oranges yet — perfect, that’s section F’s job, and you should say so out loud: “hold that complaint, you’re about to be able to answer it.”

title: The Beam Balance
text:
🧪 Bench it: find the banana

6 🍊 = 3 🍌. Take away one banana from the right. What must you take off the left to keep it level?
Try 1 orange. Tips. Try 2 oranges. Level.



One banana = two oranges, and nobody told you. You weighed it. The beam is a machine for finding things out. 🔍

title: The Beam Balance
text:
What “3 apples” actually means
\[3 \text{ apples} \;=\; \text{apple} + \text{apple} + \text{apple}\]

\[3 \times 2 \;=\; 2 + 2 + 2 \;=\; 6\]


Multiplication is a shortcut for adding the same thing over and over. That’s the whole definition.


⏱️ Time: 10 minutes

title: The Beam Balance
text:
But is \(3 \times 2\) the same as \(2 \times 3\)?


3 rows of 2
● ●
● ●
● ●
\(2 + 2 + 2 = 6\)

2 rows of 3
● ● ●
● ● ●
\(3 + 3 = 6\)




Turn the paper sideways 🔄

It’s the same dots. Nobody added one, nobody took one away. You just rotated it. That’s why the order never matters.



Hand out squared paper or use bricks in a rectangle and physically rotate it 90°. This beats every algebraic argument for commutativity at this age: it is a proof they can see, and it takes eight seconds. Resist the temptation to prove it by splitting numbers into ones — that argument is correct but it loses the room.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
Multiply the whole beam

2 oranges balance 1 banana.   Double both pans.   Still level?



\(2\,🍊 = 1\,🍌\)  →  \(4\,🍊 = 2\,🍌\) ✅
Triple it: \(6\,🍊 = 3\,🍌\). That’s the puzzle from section D. Same beam all along.




You can multiply both sides by anything and the beam stays level, because you did the same amount to each. Multiply one side only and it tips, same as always.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
What is ONE melon worth?

🍉🍉  ⚖️  🍊🍊🍊🍊🍊🍊
Two melons balance six oranges. I don’t want two melons. I want one.


Split both pans into 2 equal groups
\[\frac{2\,🍉}{2} = \frac{6\,🍊}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 1\,🍉 = 3\,🍊\]



That’s division. And notice what just happened: you got the beam down to one of the thing you were asking about. That is what grown-ups call solving. You’ve been doing it for ten minutes. 🎓


⏱️ Time: 12 minutes

title: The Beam Balance
section: The move you will use for the rest of your life
text:
The move you will use for the rest of your life


To find one of something

Divide both sides by how many you’ve got.



Stuck with 2 melons? Divide both sides by 2.
Stuck with 5 melons? Divide both sides by 5.
Stuck with 27.6 of something? …you can already see where this is going. 👀



Do not present division as “the opposite of multiplication” and then re-derive the melon result separately — that spends the budget twice on one idea. Division IS the isolate-the-unknown move, taught in one breath. The last bullet is the hinge into section G; pause on it and let someone say 27.6 out loud before you advance.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
The real question

One wheel turn rolls 27.6 cm. You want to drive 30 cm. How many motor degrees?


Call the number of turns \(t\). That’s the thing you don’t know yet.
\[27.6 \times t \;=\; 30\]
“27.6 oranges’ worth of turns balances 30.” It’s the melon puzzle with worse handwriting.


Insist that they name the unknown before touching it. “The thing I don’t know yet gets a letter” is the entire conceptual leap into algebra, and it costs nothing here because the beam has already made the unknown feel like a physical object sitting in a pan.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
Solve it on the beam

I’m stuck with 27.6 of them. Divide both sides by 27.6: \[t = \frac{30}{27.6} \approx 1.087 \text{ turns}\]
But the motor doesn’t count turns, it counts degrees. One turn is 360°. So multiply both sides by 360: \[360 \times t = 360 \times 1.087 \approx \mathbf{391°}\]



Two moves. ÷ 27.6 on both sides, × 360 on both sides. Nobody handed you 391. ✅

title: The Beam Balance
text:
Write your own formula

\[\text{degrees} \;=\; \frac{\text{distance}}{27.6} \times 360\]


Or, for any wheel on Earth
\[\text{degrees} \;=\; \frac{\text{distance}}{\pi \times d} \times 360\]
Put any distance in. Get degrees out. This is the tool. 🧰

title: The Beam Balance
text:
Same answer, two roads


Yesterday: the recipe
\(360 \div 27.6 \approx 13.04°\)/cm
\(30 \times 13.04 \approx 391°\)

Today: the beam
\(t = 30 \div 27.6 \approx 1.087\)
\(1.087 \times 360 \approx 391°\)



Identical. Yesterday’s shortcut was this beam with the working rubbed out. Now you know why it’s allowed, and you can rebuild it when you forget it. 🔁

title: The Beam Balance
text:
🎯 Prove it on three distances






At your bench


Do all three on paper first, then run them and tape-measure.



Distance
Your degrees
Measured




100 cm
?



42 cm
?



17 cm
?








Answers: 1304°, 548°, 222°. Notice 1304. That’s yesterday’s number, and today it’s yours.

⏱️ Time: 12 minutes

Rounding: 42/27.6 × 360 = 547.8, and 17/27.6 × 360 = 221.7. Accept anything within a degree or two — the point is the method, and the encoder can’t tell the difference anyway. Expect the measured column to be slightly short on every row; that’s backlash and coast, which is D3’s and D4’s business, not a mistake in their algebra. Say so, or they’ll distrust the maths they just built.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
Today’s gate






You’re done when…



You can take a beam from \(27.6 \times t = 30\) to 391° with no help
You can explain why removing one object from each side of \(6\,🍊 = 3\,🍌\) makes it tip
You can produce the degrees for a distance I make up on the spot





Next: your robot drives straight lines, and then we ask it to turn a corner. 📐


Gate leg two is the one to actually check per student; legs one and three will pass for students who have merely memorised a recipe, and leg two won’t. Ask it as a one-line oral question at the bench. Then tease D3: the sides of the square will hold beautifully with today’s degree maths, and the corners will still walk away — because a turn is not a distance.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
🏠 The Catch-Up Lab ⚖️






If you missed this session, start here


⚖️ Open the Beam Balance Catch-Up Lab →
The whole lesson, on your own, in about 45 minutes. Every beam move is locked behind a tip-or-level prediction, so you still get to break the rule yourself instead of watching someone else break it. No robot needed until the last step.




Missed the class? Work all 13 steps. It ends with the same gate you’d have been asked at the bench.
Were you here? Jump to the last step, the free-play beam with every button unlocked.

Its beam runs honest arithmetic (count × true-worth per pan) and renders the pans as countable fruit, which is what makes object-vs-amount visible: 6 🍊 and 3 🍌 sit level while looking nothing alike. The robot puzzle deliberately can’t draw 27.6 wheels, so that pan degrades to 27.6 × t — the abstraction step, shown rather than asserted. If you send an absent student here, still check gate leg two orally when they’re back; the lab makes them type it and self-mark, which is weaker than you asking.

title: The Beam Balance
text:
🏠 Take it further

Invent a fruit worth 4 oranges. Write a beam for it. Can a friend solve it?
\(5\,🍉 = ?\,🍊\). You know one melon is 3 oranges, so multiply both sides.
Work backwards: your robot drove 391°. How far did it go? Same beam, other direction.



The beam works both ways. That’s the point of a balance: it never cared which side you started from. ⚖️

title: Your Library — the Cheat Sheet
text:
File
What it knows about




movements.py
wheels and the eye — driving, turning, finding the mat


claw_gripper.py
a claw — jaws that close sideways


lift_gripper.py
a fork — an arm that scoops upward



You get one movements.py and as many gripper files as you built mechanisms — one, or both.
One import line per mechanism you actually built. Give each one a name:
from movements import *
import claw_gripper as claw      # port E
import lift_gripper as lift      # port C

claw.grab()      # the jaws close
lift.grab()      # the fork rises
Built only one? Then one line, and gripper is the natural name:
import claw_gripper as gripper   # ...or lift_gripper






WarningTwo mechanisms on the SAME port is the one thing that can’t work



The two gripper files already default to a port each — the claw to E, the lift to C. If a mechanism won’t answer, check CLAW_PORT and LIFT_PORT first, before you touch anything else.



🏷️ Why as claw and not from claw_gripper import *? Because with two mechanisms, a star import is a silent trap: import both files and the second grab overwrites the first. You’d get one working verb, one dead one, and no error message. claw.grab() and lift.grab() can’t collide — you said which one you meant.
It also tells you which file to open when something misbehaves, and it makes rebuilding a claw as a fork a one-word change on the import line.
Driving is different: there’s only one movements.py, so nothing can shadow it and import * is safe. Star-import a file when it’s the only one of its kind. Name it when something else could claim the same words.

title: Your Library — the Cheat Sheet
text:
The rules of the road
Distances in mm. Speeds in mm/s. Turning takes a flag.
drive_straight(300) drives 30 cm. drive_straight(300, speed=150) does it slowly. Turning is Pybricks’ own verb, and one word decides everything:
robot.turn(90)                   # BY 90, from wherever I'm pointing
robot.turn(90, absolute=True)    # TO heading 90 on the mat

🧭 Absolute is a compass; relative is a steering wheel. robot.turn(90, absolute=True) three times leaves you at 90 — not 270. Each absolute turn throws away the leftover error from the last one instead of inheriting it. Four relative turns pile their mistakes up until the robot walks off the mat. Write the anchor run in absolute turns; reach for the relative one only when the mission really means “a quarter turn from here”.

title: Your Library — the Cheat Sheet
text:
The verbs

Driving — movements.py



Verb
What it does




robot.reset(angle=0)
“the way I’m facing now is zero”


drive_straight(mm)
drive straight; negative = backward


robot.turn(a, absolute=True)
turn until you face heading a


robot.turn(a)
spin a degrees more, from here


robot.angle()
which way am I pointing right now


follow_line(mm)
ride the edge of the line



Turning and heading are Pybricks’ own — they already do the job, so movements.py doesn’t wrap them in a second name.


Finding the mat — the verbs that fix your position







Verb
What it does




find_line()
creep until the eye sees a line; True if found


drive_to_wall()
creep until the wheels stall on the border


wall_square(h)
push flat on the border, then declare heading h


square_on_line(h)
sit square on a line, then declare h — two eyes


show_eye()
print what the eye sees — use this to tune




👁️ One eye or two? One eye tells you that you are on the line, never whether you’re crooked on it — so a one-eye robot squares up on a wall (wall_square), where both wheels press the same flat edge. A second eye on the free port buys square_on_line(). That is the trade port A is for.

find_line() returns True or False. Check the answer.
if find_line():
    drive_straight(120)          # measured FROM the line
else:
    print("no line -- something is wrong")

🎨 The colour verbs are downstairs. find_color() and follow_line_to_color() are at the bottom of movements.py, under a STRETCH banner. You do not need them: the anchor run scores ~135 points without ever naming a colour. Reflection is one number and it barely moves; colour depends on the bulbs over the table. Get the five verbs above locked first — the colour notes are a D24 job.



Your mechanisms — claw_gripper.py and/or lift_gripper.py
Both files answer to the same verbs. Whatever you named them on the import line goes in front — gripper., claw., lift.:







Verb
What it does




gripper.home()
find the end stop, call it zero — run this first, always


gripper.grab()
close on the object and keep squeezing it


gripper.release()
open all the way and let go


gripper.release(50)
move to 50° from that mechanism’s zero; check that the object can clear




🎤 Open only as far as you need. On this claw, zero is the rigid open stop. home() finds it, sets the reading to 0°, and stays there. Plain release() returns to OPEN_TARGET = 0. A larger target such as 50° leaves the jaws less open, which can reduce their sweep near another object. Test that the chosen opening still releases your object. Each mechanism has its own reference and settings.


🎯 There is no “did I get it?” verb, and that is deliberate. If a grab comes up empty, the claw was in the wrong place — and a robot that knows it missed still has no idea where it actually is, so it can’t do anything useful about it. Spend the effort on arriving at the same spot every time instead: a wall_square() before the grab beats any amount of checking after it.


⚠️ Two mechanisms means two home() calls. Every mechanism needs its own datum, and neither one homes the other:
claw.home()
lift.home()


📦 Same three words on every robot. Four students built four different mechanisms. A claw closes sideways; a fork scoops upward; they share no parts. But the mission list can’t tell them apart —
gripper.home()
drive_straight(200)
gripper.grab()
drive_straight(-200)
gripper.release()
That list runs on all four robots. The only line that differs between them is the import. That is what a library is for: hide the machine behind the word.
Built two mechanisms? Then the name in front says which one you’re talking to — claw.grab(), lift.grab() — and the three verbs stay exactly the same.

title: Your Library — the Cheat Sheet
section: How this robot knows where it is
text:
How this robot knows where it is
Two things, and only two:

the gyro — which way you are facing
the wheels — how far you have travelled

Both drift. Every mm you drive adds a little error, and that error never goes away on its own. It just keeps adding up, all run long.
So we use the third thing: the mat. The mat is printed — its lines are in exactly the right place every single time. When the eye finds one, you know where you are again for real, instead of from adding up guesses.

🗺️ Everything above the “Finding the mat” line adds error. Everything below it takes error away. A run that never checks itself against the mat is slowly getting lost and doesn’t know it.


The two things that fix your run
find_line() / follow_line() — position truth, from the printed mat. Drive to a landmark, then measure from there. A leg that ends on a found line doesn’t care about the wheel slip that happened on the way to it.
gripper.home() — the same idea, for your mechanism
The motor counts degrees from a mark on its own shaft — it has never seen your claw. Skip a gear tooth in a crash, re-seat an axle, or re-gear the mechanism, and the mark stays where it was while your jaws move. That zero is now garbage, and every run_target after it inherits the mistake. More on that pair of verbs.
So don’t guess. Drive it until it physically can’t move, and call that zero.
claw.control.limits(torque=HOME_TORQUE)
claw.run_until_stalled(-CLOSE_SPEED, then=Stop.COAST)
wait(200)
claw.reset_angle(0)
claw.control.limits(torque=GRIP_TORQUE)
The printed mat never lies — neither does the end stop. Same trick, two places: stop guessing, go and touch something that is where it says it is.
That works because the end stop is rigid and always in the same place. An object in the jaws is neither — which is why grab() does something different. See below.

⚠️ Your heading has no landmark. find_line() fixes how far you’ve travelled, but nothing on this robot re-checks which way you’re pointing — that’s the gyro alone, for the whole run. So place the robot straight in the start area, call robot.reset(angle=0) once, and keep your legs short.

Move by, or move to
run_angle and run_target — two verbs, one word of difference in what they mean, and your mechanism lives or dies on it.

run_target(300, 150)




you say
“turn 150° more”
“go to 150”

wherever it is right now

the second one does nothing


shoved by hand
inherits the shove
drives back out of it




🧭 You already know this pair — it’s the same idea, twice. On the wheels it’s a flag: robot.turn(90) moves by, robot.turn(90, absolute=True) moves to. On a motor it’s two verb names: run_angle moves by, run_target moves to. Different hardware, different spelling, one rule: a relative move inherits every mistake before it, an absolute move forgets them.


🤖 Wheels move by. Mechanisms move to. A wheel can roll forever, so “300 mm more” is a sensible thing to want. A claw has a small number of places it is allowed to be — open, gripping, stowed — so every verb in your gripper file is run_target.


⚠️ run_target ignores the sign of the speed. The target picks the direction, so run_target(-300, 0) and run_target(300, 0) do exactly the same thing. Every other verb you own — run, run_angle, run_until_stalled — uses a negative speed to mean “the other way”. This one doesn’t. Want to go the other way? Change the target.


🎯 And zero is not yours. Motor(Port.E) starts counting from a mark on the motor shaft, not from your jaws — the motor has never seen your claw. Skip a gear tooth, re-seat an axle, or re-gear the mechanism, and the mark stays put while your jaws move. That’s why home() is line one.

title: Your Library — the Cheat Sheet
section: Stall to find zero — torque to hold a thing
text:
Stall to find zero — torque to hold a thing
Your mechanism does two jobs that look the same — press until something stops you — and they need opposite tools. Getting them the wrong way round is what makes a claw let go halfway across the mat.



The job
The question
The tool




home()
where is my claw?
stall into the end stop


grab()
how hard do I squeeze?
ask for a torque




Finding zero — run_until_stalled
motor.run_until_stalled(-CLOSE_SPEED, then=Stop.COAST, duty_limit=HOME_EFFORT)
motor.reset_angle(0)                    # the jaws just met -- THAT is zero







Part
What it’s for




speed
direction and how fast. Negative = the other way.


then=Stop.COAST
relax on arrival. Homing is leaving, not holding.


duty_limit
how hard it may push, 0–100.




🧱 Stalling is only trustworthy against a thing that doesn’t move. The jaws meeting each other is rigid, part of the mechanism, and in exactly the same place on every run. Press into that and you get the same answer every time. That’s what makes home() exact.
An object is none of those things. It sits where it landed, it squashes, it rolls. Press into that and “where it stopped” is a different number every run — which is why gripping needs the other tool.


🎯 Zero goes where the jaws meet. Both gripper files home the jaws shut and call that 0, so every angle in the file reads as how far open the mechanism is. READY_ANGLE is a positive number and GRIP_TARGET a small negative one. Nothing to measure, nothing to mistype, and nothing to re-measure after you re-gear.


⚠️ duty_limit is the knob that breaks gears. Too high and the motor keeps shoving after the mechanism has arrived — you’ll hear the plastic teeth skip. Too low and it gives up early, reset_angle(0) fires anyway, and now zero is almost right. It lives in your gripper file’s facts block as HOME_EFFORT (the claw starts at 40 — it is pressing jaw on jaw — and the lift at 75) — change it there, never at the call, and adjust by ear.



Holding a thing — aim past it, cap the torque
claw.control.limits(torque=GRIP_TORQUE)     # the squeeze, set once
claw.run_target(CLOSE_SPEED, GRIP_TARGET, then=Stop.HOLD, wait=False)
GRIP_TARGET is deliberately set a little past where the jaws meet. The claw can never get there — the object is in the way — so it never stops trying, and it leans in at GRIP_TORQUE for the whole carry.

🧮 GRIP_TARGET is a small negative number, and that’s the whole trick. Zero is where the jaws meet, so “a few degrees past shut” is just -10 — the same line in every squad’s file, with nothing to measure and nothing to keep it in step with.


🤝 Why aim at a place you can’t reach? Because that’s what keeps the pressure on. A motor that arrives stops pushing: it holds the angle it reached, and the moment the object settles a hair, your squeeze is gone and the object walks out on the next turn. A motor that’s still trying takes up that slack by itself.
This is also why grab() never calls hold() — freezing the claw where it is would undo the entire trick.


🔩 GRIP_TORQUE is one number doing two jobs. It’s how hard you squeeze, and it’s the gear protection: the motor physically cannot shove harder than this, whatever you ask it. Raise it if the object slips on turns; lower it if you hear crunching or the object deforms. Find it on the mat, with the object you actually carry — not by guessing at the desk.

title: Your Library — the Cheat Sheet
section: Three ways to move a motor
text:
Three ways to move a motor
You’ve met all three. Here’s when to reach for which.









What you say
What you get




motor.run(300)
“spin at 300 deg/s”
one wheel, exact speed


robot.straight(300)
“drive 30 cm”
both wheels, gyro-straight, ramped


motor.dc(40)
“40% power”
no promise at all




🔋 We don’t compete on dc(). dc(40) on a fresh battery, a tired battery, and a carpet seam is three different robots. run(300) is the same robot every time — it spends whatever power it takes to hold 300 deg/s. WRO runs are won by doing the same thing twice, and that’s the one thing raw power can’t promise.


⚖️ Same rule, over in the claw. GRIP_TORQUE is in mNm — an amount of actual turning force — for exactly the reason run() is in deg/s: ask for the thing you want and the hub spends whatever power that costs today. Percentages are a promise about the battery. Units are a promise about the robot.

DriveBase (robot.straight, robot.turn) does the most for you: it converts mm to degrees, holds the gyro line, and ramps up and down so nothing lurches. Use it for driving — every verb in movements.py is built on it.
motor.run_until_stalled() and motor.run_target() are what your gripper file uses — a claw hunts an end stop or goes to an angle; it never just spins. Plain motor.run() is what you’d reach for if you ever needed one drive wheel moving on its own: DriveBase always moves both, so the shortcut never completely replaces the motors underneath it.

title: The Earned Shortcut
text:
Break it: the merge 🔥

Your team just picked its robot, and it’s not yours. Your movements.py thinks the wheels are 88 mm, and the chosen robot’s are 87. Your teammate’s turn kp is tuned hotter. A motor sits on a different port. How many edits until your mission runs on this robot?


  
    sara/movements.py
    WHEEL_MM = 88
    KP = 4
    left = Motor(Port.A)
  
  
    omar/movements.py
    WHEEL_MM = 87
    KP = 6
    left = Motor(Port.B)
  
  
    lena/movements.py
    WHEEL_MM = 90 😱
    KP = 3.5
    left = Motor(Port.A)
  
  🤖ONE robot



Every file was tuned for a robot that just became a parts donor. The facts (wheels, ports, gains, speeds) are scattered across files and functions, so a robot swap means twenty hunted edits, and missing one means the robot lies quietly. The facts need one home.



Make it concrete with the team’s actual files if the draft order allows — three real constants blocks on screen beats the mock-up. Sharpen the sting: it’s not just today’s merge. The donor pool means a swap can happen again mid-season (a cracked chassis at Week 4 pace), and next time there’s no afternoon to spare. Elicit the shape of the fix before naming it — they’ve done this twice: constants block (square day), library module (consolidation day). Same instinct, one level up: promote the constants to a single shared object the whole team’s code reads.

title: The Earned Shortcut
section: Fix it: ROBOT FACTS, the robot in one place
text:
Fix it: ROBOT FACTS, the robot in one place
# movements.py -- ROBOT FACTS. The only place a number about the robot lives.
LEFT_MOTOR_PORT  = Port.F     # yours; re-port a motor = one edit
RIGHT_MOTOR_PORT = Port.B     # yours
EYE_PORT         = Port.D     # yours

LEFT_DIRECTION  = Direction.COUNTERCLOCKWISE   # flip if it reverses  TUNE
RIGHT_DIRECTION = Direction.CLOCKWISE                             # TUNE

WHEEL_DIAMETER = 88           # mm, MEASURE the team robot        TUNE
AXLE_TRACK     = 128          # mm, wheel centre to centre        TUNE

CRUISE_SPEED   = 300          # mm/s
LINE_THRESHOLD = 50           # halfway between black and white  TUNE
KP_LINE        = 1.2          # how hard to steer back to the line TUNE


One block at the top of the file, a name on every line, TUNE on everything you must measure. Nothing further down is allowed to know a number about the robot. It reads the block. Same instinct you’ve used twice already, one level up.



No classes today, and none this season — a plain block of named constants does the whole job, and every student can already read one. Walk the categories: ports, geometry, tuned knobs — point out these are exactly the numbers that differed across the three files on the last slide. Make TUNE the habit: it marks every value that must be measured on this robot, so a squad scanning the block knows exactly what a robot swap costs them. The full gold-reference block is in code/movements.py; teams copy it and edit their measured values.

title: The Earned Shortcut
text:
Every verb reads the block
# movements.py -- the verbs READ the block, they don't hide numbers
left_motor  = Motor(LEFT_MOTOR_PORT, LEFT_DIRECTION)
right_motor = Motor(RIGHT_MOTOR_PORT, RIGHT_DIRECTION)

robot = DriveBase(left_motor, right_motor,
                  WHEEL_DIAMETER, AXLE_TRACK)

def drive_straight(distance_mm, speed=CRUISE_SPEED):
    robot.settings(straight_speed=speed)
    robot.straight(distance_mm)


New robot? Measure it, edit the block, done. The library and every mission file never change, and the donor pool just became a one-line insurance policy. 🛡️



The team exercise that proves it (from the exemplar): run the merged code with teammate A’s old constants on the chosen robot — watch the square miss; then fix ONLY the ROBOT FACTS block and rerun — the square closes. One file changed, zero functions touched. That felt difference is the lesson. Also flag the discipline cost honestly: from today, hard-coding a number inside a function is a team foul — a merge conflict waiting to happen. The constants block habit from the library days is what made this promotion cheap. Continuity note: squads’ own movements.py from D5 may still spell the turn knob gain= — fold the rename into today’s promotion and say it once: “we’ve been calling this knob the gain; its code name is kp, same K-family as the KP constants.”

title: The Earned Shortcut
text:
You built a robot driver 🏆


You wrote, these two weeks

your turn verb, a PD turn that watches itself, brakes before it arrives, and lands true
drive_straight(distance), a self-healing straight with a finish line in degrees


Every WRO robot needs

turns that are true, not “about right”
straights that survive bumps, seams, and battery moods




Pybricks ships both moves, polished and tested, inside one tool: DriveBase. It runs a professional P·I·D on every move, and you’ll understand every letter of it, because you spent two weeks building all three.



This is the payoff the whole fortnight has been walking toward — let it feel like a gift, not a rug-pull. The frame that keeps their work dignified: professionals don’t hand-roll what a trusted library ships, but they can only trust it because they know what’s inside — and this room now does. If anyone asks “why didn’t we start here?”: because then DriveBase would be magic, and magic can’t be debugged at a competition table. Nothing they built was wasted — the next slides show exactly which verbs survive.

title: The Earned Shortcut
text:
Measure your robot first

DriveBase asks for two numbers: wheel diameter and axle track (tire-center to tire-center). Why does it need the second one?
Hint: you already used it once, back when you drove a square…



It’s your turn-circle! You ran that math by hand once to get 131, and DriveBase runs your derivation for any angle. The shortcut is math you already own.



Both numbers are measured, not copied: roll the wheel 5 turns, divide by 5 and π for diameter (they’ll land near 88); the track they measured on Day 3 for the 131 derivation (≈128 mm on the coach’s build; the stock ADB is ≈114) — have each team re-measure its chosen robot now, since that’s the number going into its config. Wrong track → every turn systematically over- or under-shoots: that’s the afternoon’s tuning conversation (robot.settings()). If asked why the track matters: a spin-in-place drives the wheels around a circle as wide as the axle track — wider track = more wheel-degrees per robot-degree.

title: The Earned Shortcut
section: Build your DriveBase from the block
text:
Build your DriveBase from the block
from pybricks.robotics import DriveBase   # now earned

robot = DriveBase(left_motor, right_motor,
                  WHEEL_DIAMETER, AXLE_TRACK)
robot.use_gyro(True)  # your gyro + full PID, switched on
robot.settings(straight_speed=CRUISE_SPEED)

DriveBase speaks mm and robot-degrees, as in robot.straight(300) and robot.turn(90). With use_gyro(True) every move is watched and PID-corrected, exactly like yours were. Its two constructor arguments are the two facts you measured: wheel diameter and axle track.

title: The Earned Shortcut
text:
✂️ Now delete your turn verb

Your turn(angle, absolute=False) from the library days. Here is Pybricks’:

robot.turn(angle, then=Stop.HOLD, wait=True, absolute=False)


The same word, the same default, the same meaning: robot.turn(90) spins 90 more, robot.turn(90, absolute=True) faces 90. You didn’t guess it, you re-derived it, because it’s the only sensible way to say it. (Pybricks puts absolute last, after then= and wait=, so always name it: absolute=True, never a bare True.)




So the verb goes. A function that only re-spells a built-in is one more name to maintain, so delete it and call robot.turn(). movements.py keeps the verbs that do real work: drive_straight, find_line, follow_line, drive_to_wall, wall_square, square_on_line.



This is the moment the fortnight pays off twice — don’t rush it. Put their D5 turn on screen beside the Pybricks line and let the room notice the match before you say it; the “we invented the same thing” feeling is what makes the deletion satisfying instead of deflating. Then make the rule explicit and general, because it governs every file they write from here: a wrapper has to earn its name. If a function only renames something Pybricks already gives you, it is one more thing to keep in sync and one more name for a teammate to learn — delete it. If it holds real logic (hunting a line, feeling a wall), keep it. Same test kills the heading() wrapper someone always proposes: robot.angle() already says it. Expect one squad to object that “our name is friendlier” — the answer is that the friendly name is now wrong half the time, because theirs took no then= or wait=. Land the positional trap explicitly, because it bites silently: in their version absolute was the 2nd argument, in Pybricks’ it is the 4th, so robot.turn(90, True) sets then=True and turns relative anyway. The habit that makes it a non-issue is one they already have from speed= and kd= — name the argument.

title: The Earned Shortcut
text:
Why the shortcut is team-proof
DriveBase reads the same block, so the pro tool is per-robot too. And it hands you three things your library already wanted:







It gives you
Your library uses it for




robot.settings()
speeds and accelerations, the pro version of your tuned constants


robot.stalled()
drive_to_wall() · wall_square(), feeling the border


robot.distance()
a free odometer that every hunting verb measures with





Nothing here is a new idea. It’s your own three needs, already built. 🧰



Two acts of the day snap together here: the reveal is wired straight into the ROBOT FACTS block, so the shortcut is born team-proof. robot.settings() is the pro version of their tuned constants — speeds and accelerations, adjustable per robot, stored in the block. Also worth naming: robot.stalled() is what drive_to_wall and wall_square are built on, and robot.distance() is a free odometer. Don’t tour the whole API — the duel is next; let the tool prove itself.
