title: The Earned Shortcut
text:
What retires, what stays yours


Retires today 🪦

your turn verb → robot.turn(…)
the hand-tuned turn kp/kd → DriveBase’s own PID
hub.imu.reset_heading(0) → robot.reset(angle=0)


Stays in movements.py 💪

drive_straight(), new insides and the same name
drive_to_wall() · wall_square(), the feel verbs
follow_line() · square_on_line(), the eyes verbs
every mechanism verb Week 3 will add




DriveBase replaces the moving and nothing else. It has no idea how to feel a wall, ride a line’s edge, or work a mechanism. From here on: DriveBase drives, your library does the rest.



This boundary slide is the anti-demoralizer — put numbers on it: two verbs retire, five survive today, and every mechanism verb from Week 3 joins the surviving side. Be precise about how they retire, because the two cases differ. drive_straight keeps its name: it still does real work (it sets the speed, then drives), so its insides swap to robot.straight() and every mission list runs unchanged — that’s the payoff of naming moves, swap the engine and keep the verb. The turn verb is the other case: robot.turn() already takes the same absolute flag, so wrapping it would add a name and nothing else — it is deleted, not rewrapped. robot.stalled() upgrades the inside of drive_to_wall without changing its name, same as drive_straight. Name one more so nobody is surprised later: square_on_line changes shape inside. The version they wrote on the line day drives both wheels and lets each one park itself the moment its own eye crosses — which works because those were two independent motors. Once the motors belong to a DriveBase, starting one stops the other, so the library version creeps until either eye finds the line and then pivots to bring the second one on. Same verb, same reason it needs two eyes, different insides — and that difference is itself the lesson about what you traded away for DriveBase’s gyro. Last, the zero: from today hub.imu.reset_heading(0) is the wrong verb — DriveBase owns the gyro now, so robot.reset(angle=0) is what says “this way is zero”, and it moves the gyro and the odometer together. Say it out loud, because every program they wrote in the last fortnight opens with the old line, and a squad that keeps it ends up with two zeros that disagree.

title: The Earned Shortcut
text:
Mini Mission 🎤






The challenge


A 3-task run (drive, turn, push an object home) in 60 seconds. Everything from two weeks on one clock: integration, time management, nerve.




Plan it as a sequence of your verbs, written out longhand. The list that walks itself is still ahead of you.
Budget the clock: a clean 2-task run beats a chaotic 3-task attempt. (Sound familiar? It’s the anchor-first rule, in miniature.)


Template is Competition Ready Lesson 8 “Mission Ready.” This is the last solo competition and the scorecard’s final data point — watch integration and composure, not just score. Call out anyone who deliberately drops to two tasks to bank clean points: that’s competition maturity, praise it loudly — it’s the exact instinct the anchor-first strategy needs from them in Week 4. After scores are recorded, close the leaderboard era warmly: from tomorrow the competition is team vs team.

title: The Earned Shortcut

The draft 🤝

Teams are formed on who works well together and what each team needs. Complementary skills beat matching skills.
Each team reviews its members’ robots and selects one as its competition robot.
The unselected robots become the parts donor pool, your insurance one config edit away. 🛡️
From tomorrow: team vs team, every day, which doubles the mat time.



Your robot may retire to the donor pool. Your code and your skills don’t. Everything merges onto the team robot through one ROBOT FACTS block, and both of the team’s cross-trained roles need every verb you built. The draft picks a chassis, not a coder.



Say the framing line exactly as planned and nothing more: “I’m teaming you based on who works well together and what each team needs” — never rank, never “you scored lowest.” The pairings are already decided from the private scorecard + library benchmarks; announce, don’t debate. Give the selection its dignity: each team physically inspects its candidate robots (the four quality checks from Day 1 make a nice ritual return) before choosing. Handle the sting of an unselected robot with the card’s line — the donor pool is genuinely valuable, not a consolation. Set up team build areas after the announcement.

Before we code

✅ Re-run the four checks: click · twin · shake · roll.
🔋 Battery light green-ish? You’ll see why that matters today.

title: Make It Move
text:
Unplugged: drive a blindfolded partner






The game


One of you is the programmer, and your blindfolded partner is the robot. Only separate commands: “forward 30 cm,” “turn 90° right.” No steering, no touching. Get your robot across the mat to the target.




Give the commands. Watch where your “robot” actually ends up.
Swap roles and run it again.

title: Make It Move
text:
What just went wrong?


You commanded

forward 30 cm
turn 90°
forward 30 cm


The robot did

forward ~34 cm
turn ~80°
forward 30 cm… into the wrong spot




That gap is open-loop drift: moving without checking the result. Your LEGO robot is about to do exactly the same thing.

text:
🏁 The race

  
    🏁 Race!
    ⏱ 0.0 s
  
  
    🚗
    6 m in 3 s
  
  
    🚙
    3 m in 3 s
  
  




Same start. Same 3 seconds. What did you notice?




…and how much faster is 🚗?




“A lot” is not a measurement.



Run the race two or three times. Elicit, don’t tell: “What did you notice?” (Car A got farther / arrived first.) “Yes — what do we call that?” SPEED. “You’re scientists now — and scientists need an accurate way to describe speed. Suggestions?” Guide toward: how far it went… and how long it took. The moment someone says “distance and time,” celebrate it — the next slide is their idea, formalized.

text:
Say it with numbers


🚗 Car A: 6 m in 3 s
→ 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m every second

🚙 Car B: 3 m in 3 s
→ 3 ÷ 3 = 1 m every second



speed = distance ÷ time: how far you get per second. That’s the whole formula, and you invented it.



Anchor with everyday speeds: a car does 100 km/h — 100 km of distance for every hour. Ask: what’s YOUR walking speed? (~5 km/h ≈ 1.4 m/s.) Then shrink to robot scale: centimeters per second.

from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor
from pybricks.parameters import Port, Direction
from pybricks.tools import wait

hub = PrimeHub()
left = Motor(Port.F, Direction.COUNTERCLOCKWISE)   # yours

left.run_time(500, 2000, wait=False)
right.run_time(500, 2000)

left.run_time(500, 2000, wait=False)   # ← tune ONLY the time
right.run_time(500, 2000)


Throw 1 lands short, throw 2 with the same number lands somewhere else?! Keep your score sheet. That wobble is evidence, and we need it later today. 🕵️

🅿️ Bonus round: The Price Is Right

title: Make It Move
text:
Quick quiz 🚨

run_time(500, 2000). You just defined speed, so 500 is a speed of what? And the 2000?
Centimeters per second? Meters? Robot points? Guess!



2000 = milliseconds. That’s how long it runs. 500 = degrees per second. It is a speed (something ÷ time), but the something isn’t distance… 🤔



Ask “what speed did you just use?” — expect silence; that’s the plan. Reveal: it’s a different kind of speed. Pybricks motor commands really do take rotational (angular) speed in deg/s — that’s the motor’s own language. The next slide makes them derive it.

title: Make It Move
text:
⚙️ Motors have a speed too

  
    Motor A
    
      
    
    0.0 rotations
  
  
    ▶ Spin for 3 s
  
  
    Motor B
    
      
    
    0.0 rotations
  




No road, no distance. So count what a motor does: turns. Spin speed = rotations ÷ time. Same recipe, new ingredient.



Elicit: “This is a motor — how can we measure how fast it is?” Expect “rotations per second” — agree enthusiastically. Don’t reveal degrees yet! Ask: “But what if I want to spin only half a turn? Or a quarter?” — let them sit with that before the next slide.

title: Make It Move
section: 🧭 What about half a rotation? A quarter?
text:
🧭 What about half a rotation? A quarter?


  
  
    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
    
    
      0°
    
    
      = 0 rotation
    
  

  
  
    0°
    90° = ¼ turn
    180° = ½ turn
    270° = ¾ turn
    360° = full turn
  





0, 30, 60, 90 … 360. Ancient sky-watchers cut a full circle into 360 equal steps called degrees. The idea comes from the Babylonians (~2000 BCE), who loved multiples of 60. The Greeks spread it, and we still use it today. 🏛️



Ask: “If I want exactly half a turn, how do I write that as a number of full rotations?” (0.5 — messy fractions ahead!) Reveal: that’s why we use degrees. Walk through the dial: 90° = quarter, 180° = half, 360° = full. Then fun history: Babylonians, base-60, ~360 days in a year — they made 360 the magic number. Greeks (Hipparchus, Ptolemy) adopted and spread it. LEGO engineers still follow that 4000-year-old choice.

title: Make It Move
text:
Name your numbers: variables
DRIVE_SPEED = 500   # deg/s
DRIVE_TIME = 2000   # ms

left.run_time(DRIVE_SPEED, DRIVE_TIME, wait=False)
right.run_time(DRIVE_SPEED, DRIVE_TIME)

Name a number once → change it in one place → every move retunes. First habit of clean robot code.

title: Make It Move
text:
🎯 Mission: drive exactly 100 cm

Your robot only listens to deg/s and ms. How do you order it to travel 100 cm?
Think: what’s the only part of the robot that actually touches the mat?



The wheel 🛞. Every degree the motor turns becomes distance on the ground.

title: Make It Move
text:
🛞 Unroll the wheel


  Tiny wheel: rope around the rim = 8 cm
  
  
  
    
      
      
      
    
  
  
  
  1 rotation = the whole rope = 8 cm

  YOUR wheel: rope around the rim ≈ 27.6 cm
  
  
  
    
      
      
      
    
  
  
  
  1 rotation = the whole rope ≈ 27.6 cm

🛞 Roll one full turn



The rim is a rope wrapped in a circle — rolling one turn unfolds the rope flat on the ground. A wheel whose rope is 8 cm travels exactly 8 cm per rotation; your big wheel’s rope is ≈ 27.6 cm, so one rotation = 27.6 cm. Ask before rolling: “if the rope is 8 cm, how far does one rotation take you?” (Note: the two scenes use different zoom levels — each ruler is in its own wheel’s units.)

title: Make It Move
text:
From deg/s to cm/s



The Translation
Since 1 full rotation is 360° = 27.6 cm: \[360\text{ deg/s} = 27.6\text{ cm/s}\]

To convert any speed, we scale it: \[\text{Speed (cm/s)} = \text{Speed (deg/s)} \times \frac{27.6}{360}\]



Practical Example 🧮
For DRIVE_SPEED = 500:

\(500 \times \frac{27.6}{360} \approx 38.3\text{ cm/s}\)

Let’s check that claim!

title: Make It Move
text:
🔬 Speed lab: measure YOUR robot

Put tape at the front wheels. Run the program: DRIVE_SPEED = 500, DRIVE_TIME = 2000.
Measure the distance with a ruler. Write it down.
Compute: speed = distance ÷ 2 seconds. Math predicted ~38 cm/s → ~77 cm.



Got less than 77? And your neighbor got a different number from the same code?! (Hint: check both battery lights. 🔋) Commanding is not the same as getting.


⏱️ Time: 15 minutes

title: Make It Move
text:
So… exactly 100 cm?

At ~38 cm/s: time = 100 ÷ 38 ≈ 2.6 s. Set DRIVE_TIME = 2600. Run it. Measure it.
Did anyone land on 100 cm?



Short again, and different every run. Timed driving trusts the battery to keep its promise. There has to be a better way…


⏱️ Time: 10 minutes

title: Make It Move
text:
run_time vs run_angle


Live demo if time allows: run the same run_time program on a full hub and a nearly-empty hub — different distances. Then run_angle on both — same distance. The encoder inside the motor counts degrees; time doesn’t lie the same way twice.

title: Make It Move
text:
🎯 Predict-a-distance

You want exactly 100 cm. One wheel turn (360°) ≈ 27.6 cm. How many degrees?


🧮 Direct Conversion

Degrees per 1 cm:   \(1\text{ cm} = \frac{360^\circ}{27.6\text{ cm}} \approx 13.04^\circ/\text{cm}\)
For 100 cm:   \(\text{degrees} = 100\text{ cm} \times 13.04^\circ/\text{cm} \approx \mathbf{1304^\circ}\)



🤖 Try It Out
# Spin left and right motors together to go 100 cm
left.run_angle(DRIVE_SPEED, 1304, wait=False)
right.run_angle(DRIVE_SPEED, 1304)

⏱️ Time: 10 minutes

title: Make It Move
text:
Diameter → circumference



circumference = π × diameter. Your wheel: 3.14 × 8.8 cm ≈ 27.6 cm. For any wheel, read the diameter off the tire and multiply by π.

title: Make It Move
text:
🧪 Bonus: discover π yourself

Wrap a string around anything round: a cup, a tape roll, a bottle, your wheel. That’s C.
Measure straight across the middle. That’s d.
Divide: C ÷ d = ?



≈ 3.14, every single time. That number is π, the circle’s built-in constant. You didn’t memorize it, you discovered it.

title: Make It Move
section: 🧪 Bonus: another way to measure a circle
text:
🧪 Bonus: another way to measure a circle
No string? Catch the circle with straight lines instead.

  
    
      
    
    
    
    d = 1
    
      
    
  
  
    A square's rope needs no π:perimeter = 4 × side
    
      Outside square: 4 × 1 = 4
      → circle's rope is less than 4
    
    
      Inside square: rope ≈ 2.83
      → circle's rope is more than 2.83
    
  



2.83 < π < 4, trapped with no string needed. It is a loose trap, though. How do we squeeze it tighter? More sides →



Optional enrichment — no gate depends on it; skip live if time is tight and point kids to it for home. Build: squares are the shapes we can measure (4 × side, no π). Click 1: outside square (side = d = 1) → its rope is 4, and the circle’s rope is clearly shorter. Click 2: inside square → rope ≈ 2.83, circle clearly longer. Don’t derive the 2.83 (side = d/√2) — the picture is the proof. Since d = 1, rope ÷ d IS π, so the trap holds π itself. The “more sides” question is the cliffhanger into the demo.

title: Make It Move
text:
🧪 Bonus: Archimedes’ squeeze

  
    
    
    
    
    d = 1
  
  
    
      4
      6
      12
      24
      96
    
    4 sides
    
      2.8284
       < π < 
      4.0000
    
    real π = 3.14159…
  




Archimedes (Syracuse, ~250 BCE) did exactly this by hand, doubling up to 96 sides, and proved 3 10/71 < π < 3 1/7. He squeezed π out of a circle 2,200 years before calculators. 🏛️



Optional enrichment, self-guided at home. The inner rope (teal) is always too short, the outer (coral) always too long — the circle’s rope is trapped between them, and since d = 1 the trap holds π itself. Click 4 → 96 and watch both numbers march toward 3.14159. At 96 sides the trap is 3.1410–3.1427 — Archimedes’ actual stopping point. Connect back: the Babylonians gave us degrees, Archimedes gave us π — both live inside every wheel calculation the robot does.

Radar Gun 📡






The challenge


Predict, then prove. Measure your robot’s speed, then tell the judge exactly how many seconds it needs to cross the 1.5 m finish line. The judge starts the stopwatch, and the closest prediction wins. 3 attempts, best counts.




Pure science: measure → calculate → predict → test.
Pro move: does your prediction survive a battery swap? 😏

You own
Built on

drive_straight · turn

the turn · the straight

brakes before overshoot

A script is blind. Today: see → decide → steer. Brightness only, colour names come in Week 4.




⏱️ Time: 5 minutes, then a bug hunt

Anchor today in what they already own, or it feels like a brand-new mountain (it isn’t — the plan flags the line day as the longest precisely because the old material was video-paced; live, it’s one formula applied a third time). text:
🔎 Bug hunt: the tune that didn’t stick
def make_it_sharper():
    KP = 12          # crank steering for the whole library… right?

make_it_sharper()
drive_straight(300)  # …still lazy. Nothing changed. 😤

title: Line King
text:
Meet the eye 🔦
A flashlight + light meter in one brick. It measures its own echo.

  
    
      
      
      
    
    
    reflection() → 10
    reflection() → 88
    
    
      
      
    
    
      
      
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    black line: echo swallowed
    white mat: echo bounces back
    same flashlight,
    different echo
  

from pybricks.pupdevices import ColorSensor

left_eye = ColorSensor(Port.D)    # yours
right_eye = ColorSensor(Port.A)   # yours -- only if you fitted a second eye

left_eye.reflection()   # 0-100: % of its OWN light echoing back
left_eye.color()        # a name: Color.RED... (Week 4's tool)


Anything that changes the echo changes the number: ✨ gloss · 💡 light · 📏 height.



The live demo beats the diagram: run a print(left_eye.reflection()) loop, hold the robot, and let students slide surfaces under the eye, tilt it, lift it — the number dances. Establish the active-sensor idea: it brings its own LED, so it mostly ignores the room, but gloss, sensor height, and strong ambient light still shift the echo — which is exactly why every surface gets its own calibration (next slide). reflection() vs color(): today reflection does all the work; color() names colors and gets a cameo here — its real job is Week 4’s notes. The eye lives on port D on the coach’s robot — check yours. Following needs only one eye; square_on_line at the end of today is the job that wants a second, on the spare port A.

title: Line King
section: Break it: the threshold you guessed 🔥
text:
Break it: the threshold you guessed 🔥

Last week the tape split at 50 (white 88, black 10). Does 50 still work on the mat? The floor?

🤖 Robots out. Print reflection() across three surfaces: tape · mat · floor. Log white and black for each.


A threshold is a fact about a surface: read white · read black · split the middle.



Let each squad predict before measuring — commitments make the surprise land. The printed mat just arrived (decision #23), so this is also the real calibration-transfer checkpoint from the plan: the numbers they log here ARE the re-logged thresholds. Expected outcome: the mat’s white and the tape-field’s white read differently (print ink vs paper, matte tarp vs tape), the split point moves, and the habit lands — look first, then split what you actually see. The glossy-table failure (black reading 60, < 50 calling the line “clear” and driving over it) is the venue-day version of the same lesson; it lives as an interactive sim in the 🏠 appendix since we don’t have a glossy table in the room — mention it, don’t show it. The takeaway is a habit, not a number: re-read and re-split, every surface.

title: Line King
section: Fix it: calibrate, then decide with if / else 🎚️
text:
Fix it: calibrate, then decide with if / else 🎚️
# Calibrate FIRST -- measure, never guess
REFLECT_THRESHOLD = 50              # for THIS surface
while True:
    if left_eye.color() == Color.RED:
        hub.speaker.beep(frequency=880)     # high beep on red
    elif left_eye.reflection() < REFLECT_THRESHOLD:
        hub.speaker.beep(frequency=220)     # low beep on a line
    wait(50)
🤖 Robots out. Threshold from your mat numbers: low beep on lines, high beep on red.


if … elif is the robot choosing. New surface → re-calibrate the threshold, never the code.



This is the just-in-time concept for the day: if/elif + booleans. Keep it concrete — a boolean is the answer to a yes/no question the robot asks the world (color() == RED, reflection() < 50). elif = “otherwise, check this next.” Tie it straight back to the three-surface ritual: the threshold is data you recalibrate per surface; the if/elif structure never changes. The mat’s printed staff lines make the beeper test real mission geography — they’re the same lines we follow and square on later today. If a squad is flying, mention else for the catch-all case, but don’t gate on it.

title: Line King
text:
Ride the edge 👁️
# Watch it live FIRST -- before any steering. Just read the number.
while True:
    print("reflection:", left_eye.reflection())   # 0=black, 100=white
    wait(100)

  
    slide the eye across the edge:
    
  
  
    
    
    white mat
    black line
    
    the edge = threshold 50
    
  
  reflection 88 → error +38 · far onto white, steer hard toward the line




error = reflection − 50: + on white · − on black · 0 on the edge.



Watch reflection live on a real robot first, over white then over black — read the two numbers aloud, split them, that’s the threshold (re-do on the actual mat; venue lighting shifts it). Then the widget: drag the eye and narrate the single signed number. The key mental model is edge-following, not line-centering — one eye rides the boundary, half on black. Positive error = drifted onto white, negative = drifted onto black. This is deliberately the same shape as the gyro’s error = target − heading. Don’t mention P yet; just establish that one eye yields one clean error.

title: Line King
text:
Break it: only two answers 🔥

Two moves only: hard left or hard right. Predict the path.

while True:
    if left_eye.reflection() < THRESHOLD:
        left.run(LINE_SPEED + TURN_HARD)       # on black → yank right
        right.run(LINE_SPEED - TURN_HARD)
    else:
        left.run(LINE_SPEED - TURN_HARD)       # on white → yank left
        right.run(LINE_SPEED + TURN_HARD)
    wait(10)


Two answers means it can never go straight. It slams left-right forever.



This is bang-bang — the naïve controller. Let them predict, then confirm with the sim two slides on. The diagnosis you want in their words: “it only knows left or right, so it’s always turning.” The bridge to P is exactly the KP quiz from Day 4: what if the correction were proportional to how far off we are, instead of always full-tilt? Keep bang-bang short — it exists only to make P feel like the rescue.

title: Line King
text:
Name it: P, proportional steering 📈
error = left_eye.reflection() - THRESHOLD    # signed: how far off the edge?
left.run(LINE_SPEED + KP * error)            # far → hard steer,
right.run(LINE_SPEED - KP * error)           # near → gentle


error × KP again. Tune KP: too small = lazy, too big = the wobble is back.



The “aha” is that they’ve written this line before — twice. It’s literally the D4 self-healing straight with a new error source: swap hub.imu.heading() for the eye’s reflection and the two run lines are identical. Same error × KP, different sensor feeding it. Two failure modes to name so they recognize them on the bench: sluggish (KP too low) drifts wide on curves; twitchy (KP too high) reintroduces the wobble. Start small and adjust. This alone wins “Line King” on gentle lines — but push the speed up on a curve and it starts to overshoot, which is the doorway to the PD stretch. If a student raises the “use motor.dc()” advice here: same answer as the D4 proportional-turn coach note — run() keeps “speed” meaning speed, so KP * error stays a correction in deg/s they can reason about.

title: Line King
section: Name it: follow_line joins the library 📦
text:
Name it: follow_line joins the library 📦
def follow_line(distance_mm, speed=250, kd=0):
    """P follow on the LEFT eye. kd > 0 is the PD stretch."""
    finish = left.angle() + distance_mm * DEG_PER_MM
    last_error = 0
    while left.angle() < finish:
        error = left_eye.reflection() - THRESHOLD
        steer = KP_LINE * error + kd * (error - last_error)
        left.run(speed + steer)
        right.run(speed - steer)
        last_error = error
        wait(10)
    left.stop(); right.stop()


The P loop, bottled. A finish line in degrees makes it a segment, and kd is the stretch knob.



Same promotion ritual as every day this week: the loose P loop gets a name and moves into movements.py (its KP becomes KP_LINE — the library’s constants block already owns KP for the gyro). Map every part back to what they own: error = P on the eye, the finish line = drive_straight’s DEG_PER_MM trick (follow for a distance — that’s how missions call it), kd * (error - last_error) = the D from the library-day gyro turn, with last_error the one-line memory that makes D possible. The gate is the P version — follow_line(600) with kd=0; the stretch is sliding kd up until the fast curve stops overshooting, which is what wins Speed Demon. State the I-policy plainly and move on: integral fixes a steady offset over a long run; our segments are short, so I is a demo they can watch but never something the gate depends on.

title: Line King
text:
The two-eye job: square up 📐
The second eye’s moment: you hit a junction crooked, so sit square before the next move.
def square_on_line(speed=160):
    """Stop each wheel as ITS OWN eye reaches the line."""
    left_done = right_done = False
    left.run(speed); right.run(speed)
    while not (left_done and right_done):
        if not left_done and left_eye.reflection() < THRESHOLD:
            left.hold(); left_done = True      # park left wheel
        if not right_done and right_eye.reflection() < THRESHOLD:
            right.hold(); right_done = True    # park right wheel
        wait(5)


Each eye stops its own wheel, so the robot pivots square. That’s why it carries two.




👁️ One eye can’t do this, and it’s worth knowing why. One reading tells you that you are on the line. It never tells you whether you’re crooked on it: a robot 20° askew and a robot dead square give the same number.




So a one-eye robot squares on a wall instead. Both wheels press the same flat edge, and the edge does the aligning. Two eyes square on a line, anywhere on the mat. That’s the trade the spare port buys.



Answer the port question head-on, and answer it with our robot, not the kit: the eye is on D, the two grippers take E and C, the drive motors F and B — which leaves exactly one spare port, A. Following needs one eye; this verb wants two. So the second eye is a purchase, and A is the money. Say what it costs: spend A on an eye and you can never add a third mechanism — though the 4-motor cap (§5.2.8) was going to stop you anyway. On the real mat this kills accumulated drift in a fraction of a second, gold going into the chained runs of Week 3. (The same second eye later reads note colours in Week 4 — but never steers.)

title: Line King
text:
Line King 👑 / Speed Demon 🏁






The challenge


Line King: hold the curved line for 30 s, on accuracy and speed. Speed Demon (fast squads): the fastest run that never leaves the line.





The winning recipe

Calibrate on the mat you run on
Tune KP_LINE, then chase speed
Square at the junction to reset
(stretch) kd kills the curve overshoot


Where squads lose it

Threshold from last week’s tape, not this mat 😬
KP so high the straight wobbles
Skipping the square → drift compounds



Line King rewards a clean, honest tune over raw speed; Speed Demon is the stretch for squads whose P was solid early and who took the kd upgrade. Coach’s eye is on the tuning conversation, not the trophy: can they explain what the error means, what KP_LINE did, and why the threshold had to be re-measured on this mat? That explanation IS the gate (kd talk is stretch credit, not a requirement). Keep the taped junction handy so squaring gets used under pressure, not just demoed.

title: Line King
text:
Today’s gate






You’re done today when…



You can build, tune, and explain a P line-follower
It follows a curve reliably
Two eyes: it squares on a junction with square_on_line
One eye: you can show why it can’t, because crooked and square read the same, and the job carries to tomorrow’s wall
follow_line lives in your movements.py (it gains kd= for the PD stretch)





Next: Stop at the Wall. The motor becomes a sensor, and the wall resets the truth. 🧱


The gate is the plan’s line-day outcome: build, tune, and explain a P follower + reliable junction squaring — what the anchor run actually uses. Split the squaring half by build, because our competition robot runs one eye and square_on_line genuinely needs two: a two-eye squad demonstrates the verb, a one-eye squad demonstrates the failure (park it crooked on the line, read the number, park it square, read the same number) and carries the job to tomorrow, where wall_square solves it on the border. Do not fail a one-eye squad for a sensor it was never given. The heading= argument is tomorrow’s idea too — declaring a heading is D7’s “the wall never lies”, so name it, don’t teach it today; PD is explicitly the stretch, never the gate. A student who can narrate why each term is there owns the concept and can debug it in Week 3 when the follower serves the run. Two eyes, one job each: one follows, both square. Close by pointing forward: tomorrow the motor itself becomes a sensor — the robot feels walls, patrols between them, and resets its heading truth against them — and the scoresheet gets read the anchor-first way: everything those color-free verbs score comes first.

On a glossy venue table, “black” can bounce back 60. Drag the threshold and rescue the robot.

What will the motor move?




Next or → reveals or runs the next step. R replays, P pauses, N opens notes.


Trace the motor, yellow gears, and both linked jaws. Ask students to predict their movement before running. Positive motor movement closes this build. Keep detailed commands folded.
Run slowly. Ask students to follow the same motor through the gears to both jaws. Pause before reversing direction.

section: What if the motor turns the other way?
text:
What if the motor turns the other way?




Collect predictions before reversing. Ask whether one or both jaws will change direction.
Observe the reversal, then ask a student to trace the mechanism in their own words.

Open, stop, then close




Use the direction control. Start moving, press Stop motor, then reverse. Distinguish stopping the motor from Pause, which only freezes the demonstration. Reset scene restores this saved starting state.

How far should we open?




The dotted outline marks the fully open stop. This first physical pose is 20 degrees of motor movement away. No consistent reference has been established yet, so do not label the current motor reading with a known angle.
Reveal run_angle(OPEN_SPEED, -20). Run and observe the jaws meeting the outline. Ask what the negative sign does on this build.
Ask students why this particular movement works from this starting pose. Keep the distinction between movement amount and final position.

section: Will the same instruction work here?
text:
Will the same instruction work here?




Only the starting pose changes. Keep exactly run_angle(OPEN_SPEED, -20). Ask where the jaws will finish.
Run the unchanged instruction. The second start ends short of the open-stop outline. Ask what information is needed to choose a better movement.

section: Find the movement from the second start
text:
Find the movement from the second start




Let students adjust relative movement from the second pose. -80 reaches the outline. Compare with -20 from the first pose. The required movement depends on the start and the destination.

section: The movement amount depends on the start
text:
The movement amount depends on the start




Require students to explain why a fixed relative movement does not guarantee a fixed final opening. run_angle can work when the movement is chosen for the current start.

Where should we start counting?




Ask where we should start measuring closing positions. Let students nominate the fully open stop as a recognizable physical reference. Do not explain stall detection yet.

section: What will home() do from here?
text:
What will home() do from here?




Demonstrate the supplied operation with empty jaws. Predict where it will go first. At this point home is one usable operation; its internal code explanation stays folded.
Pause at the rigid open stop before assigning zero. Ask whether finding this position and assigning its number are the same action. Leave how the program recognizes the stop for stage 5.
Complete home(). Zero is assigned at the open stop, and the claw stays fully open there. This is both home and the ready position. Future closing targets are measured from this reference. Internal commands remain folded.

section: What changes with a different start?
text:
What changes with a different start?




Repeat home from the second starting position with empty jaws. Ask what should be the same at the end.
Pause again at the rigid open stop before zeroing. Have students compare the physical endpoint with the first run.
Complete home() from the second start. The claw finishes fully open at the same zero reference. Ask why this consistency lets us reuse closing targets.

section: Home is zero. Measure from here.
text:
Home is zero. Measure from here.




The fully open stop is both the home reference and the ready position at 0°. Homing finds that physical position and labels it zero. Ask how a closing target can now describe where to go.

section: Does a zero reading prove we found home?
text:
Does a zero reading prove we found home?




The claw is partly closed. Predict what reset_angle(0) changes. Ask whether the jaws will move.
Run reset_angle(0). The reading becomes zero while the physical jaws do not move. Ask why this zero would make our familiar target numbers refer to the wrong opening.
Run home again with empty jaws to restore zero at the fully open stop. The function finishes there. Keep its implementation folded until after the experiment.

Copy and use home()




Open the Home code control. Students can inspect and copy the complete function with its imports and constants, or download the configured starter. Ask them to paste it into their starter and call home(). Do not walk through its stall, torque, or settling commands yet.

One target, different movements




The reference is now established. A target of 60° is measured from home. Compare 0 to 60 requiring +60 and 30 to 60 requiring +30. In both cases the destination remains 60. Ask which number can stay the same.

Where will target 60° take us?




Start fully open at the homed zero reference. Reveal the prints and closing target command. Predict the jaw position when Target reached appears.
Run from 0 degrees to target 60. Follow the pending target call. Target reached prints after arrival. Mention default waiting briefly; stages 7 and 8 investigate it.

section: Will target 60° work from this start?
text:
Will target 60° work from this start?




Only the starting position changes to 30 degrees. The home reference stays the same. Predict the destination and message order before running.
Run from 30 degrees with the same reference. Both runs finish at 60 degrees, measured from home. Ask why target numbers need a consistent reference.

Find an angle that grips




One scripted comparison instead of six slides. Ask for a prediction before each trial: the button names the trial it is about to run. Every completed trial stays in the table, which is what makes the comparison visible.
The claw was homed with empty jaws, then this wide object was placed between the open jaws. The program requests the same 60° target demonstrated in stage 3, measured from home. The dotted outline marks that requested destination. Ask whether the jaws will touch the object there.
Nothing blocked the movement, so the jaws reach the requested 60° and hold it. A gap remains. This target is too small for this object. Ask what number to request instead.
Only the requested target changes, from 60 to 80. The same object and the same home reference are kept. The dotted outline now sits inside the object. Predict the angle the jaws will report when the movement ends.
Both jaws meet the object near 70°. The requested target stays 80° while the actual angle stops at 70°, and the motor task is still trying toward the destination it never reached. Contact here does not measure holding force on a real robot. Keep 80° for the next trial.
The requested target stays 80°, homed from the same reference. Only the object is narrower. Predict whether the jaws stop early again or reach the requested destination.
Nothing blocks this movement. The jaws arrive at the requested 80° and a gap remains, the same result the 60° trial gave with the wide object. The number that worked before does not work here.

section: Each object has its own contact angle
text:
Each object has its own contact angle




Three trials, one requested number each: 60° left a gap, 80° was stopped by the wide object near 70°, and the same 80° left a gap on the narrower one. Picking an exact angle for every object is impractical. Ask what the claw would need to notice instead of counting degrees.

section: Could you grip a bottle with your eyes closed?
text:
Could you grip a bottle with your eyes closed?




If a bottle were already between open fingers, could students grip it with eyes closed? Use a brief hands-on exercise or the vote buttons. Ask what would tell them they had reached the bottle. Stall has not been revealed yet.
Draw out resistance, followed by maintaining enough pressure to hold the bottle. Connect this to objects stopping the claw before its target.

section: Could the program recognize blocked movement?
text:
Could the program recognize blocked movement?




Recall an experiment in which the object stopped the jaws before the target. Predict what evidence the motor controller could use.
Run closing until blocked. Ask what the motor is still being asked to do. Explain that the controller can detect a stall when movement is obstructed.

stalled() reports blocked movement




Reveal claw.stalled() and its live indicator for the first time. It reports the controller stall detection, not what caused the blockage. Source: https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html#pybricks.pupdevices.Motor.stalled
Press once more for the reading this stage exists to establish: a stall reports blocked movement, not a held object. The object here caused it; the next slide shows the rigid open stop causing the same report with nothing to catch. Stage 9 builds a checking loop on exactly this reading, and stage 10 returns to what a stall leaves unknown.

section: How did home() recognize the open stop?
text:
How did home() recognize the open stop?




Connect this to the function students already used. home() is still folded. Let them propose using the blockage at the open stop, then open the function and read it one line at a time. Each line answers a question, and every line is revealed just above the line it protects.
Reveal claw.run_until_stalled and run it to the stall event at the rigid stop. This one instruction performs the running and the stall checking; students do not need to write a loop. It answers the slide question. Source: https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html#pybricks.pupdevices.Motor.run_until_stalled
Ask how hard the motor should push into the stop before pressing. The effort limit appears above the run, because a setting has to be chosen before the instruction that uses it. The supplied homing limit is 220 mNm, which caps how hard the motor may try. The last reveal compares the effort limits here, where the function uses them.
Ask which familiar instruction gives the stop the number zero. Let students answer before revealing reset_angle. The operation finishes and coasts, then the angle is set to 0. The jaws do not move: finding the stop supplies the physical reference, and resetting the angle labels it zero. The live stall indicator can clear once drive effort is released; the previous stall event remains the evidence.
Ask why a line that does nothing sits above the zeroing. After the coast the motor is still coming to rest, so 200 ms guarantees the number we record is the settled one. Our closing angles are found by practice runs rather than calculation, which only works if zero lands in the same place every run.
Ask whether the raised limit should stay raised. Limits persist, so home() explicitly restores the gripping limit before returning; watch the torque reading change. The jaws remain fully open at zero, and there is no further movement in home(). Open Home code to read the finished function.
Both limit lines are marked together with their values. Ask what controls how hard the motor may try, and compare HOME_TORQUE 220 mNm with GRIP_TORQUE 180 mNm: reaching the rigid stop is allowed more effort than gripping an object. A setting stays in effect until it is changed, which is why each action selects its own. The torque limit is a motor setting in mNm; this model does not measure jaw-tip force.

When will “Continue” appear?




Stage 7 follows the reference, experiment, and resistance lessons. The empty claw starts homed at the rigid open stop. Positive motor rotation closes this build. The runner supplies GRIP_TORQUE = 180 mNm. Keep stalled() visible as a familiar indicator from stage 5; done() will be introduced in stage 9. Ask when the second message will print, and take predictions aloud. Next runs the scene. Geometry and contact angles are illustrative, not calibrated robot measurements.
Let the animation finish. Follow the jaws, the pending call, and the target readout. It freezes after the second print. Playback is slowed without changing the speed constants. A presentation pause freezes model time; it does not send a motor stop command.
Ask students to explain the order: closing starts, 130° is reached, then the second print executes. Stop.HOLD maintains the reached target. Reference: https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html#pybricks.pupdevices.Motor.run_target

section: What changes when we add an object?
text:
What changes when we add an object?




The starting angle, target, speed, and Python code are unchanged. Only the object changes. Ask when the second print will appear now.
The presentation freezes after blockage is detected. The Python call remains pending: we have not made it time out or return. Navigating to a fresh trial resets the scene.
Ask: We reached the object. What is the program still waiting for? Compare actual angle near 70° with target 130°. The second message has not printed. Contact does not satisfy target arrival.

The default is wait=True




Make the implicit default visible. Adding wait=True here states the same behavior as omitting it.

What will wait=False change?




The trial resets and only the waiting argument changes. The program is now three instructions long: print, the closing command, print. Ask when the second message will print, and then ask what the program will do after that.
The second message appears immediately, while the jaws are barely open. wait=False let the program continue instead of waiting for arrival.
Press again. There is nothing left to run, so the program ends. Ending a program releases the motors, and the jaws stop at about 2° with 130° still the requested angle. Ask what the program achieved: it issued a closing command and then took it away. The motor was never given time to work. The simulator’s instruction ticks are illustrative, not firmware timing.

section: How long should the program wait?
text:
How long should the program wait?




The program needs to stay alive while the motor works, so we add a wait. Someone has to choose the number, and 200 ms sounds reasonable. Ask how far the jaws will get, and take a show of hands before running it.
The countdown beside the line runs out and the program ends with the jaws at about 42°. The object sits at 70°, so this trial ended before the claw touched anything. Nobody measured how long the closing takes; the number was a guess and the guess was short.
Ask the obvious follow-up: how much longer should it be? Any answer is another guess, and it changes with the object, the speed, and how far the jaws start from the target. Worse, a wait that is long enough still tells us nothing, because it measures time and never looks at the motor. We need to wait for the motor instead.

section: What could tell us the closing is over?
text:
What could tell us the closing is over?




Take answers before revealing any code. Recall stalled() from stage 5: it reports that the motor is being asked to move and cannot continue. Ask how a program could use it to decide when to stop waiting.
The next press replaces the fixed wait with a loop: keep waiting while the motor is not stalled. Read it aloud. wait(100) gives the movement time to begin before the first check, and wait(10) spaces the checks; neither cancels the motor task. These supplied intervals are not guarantees for every physical build. The observation wait that keeps the scene alive is left out of this excerpt.
Run it. The loop checks while the jaws close, and stalled() ends it the moment the object blocks them. The second message now appears because the closing attempt is over, not because a chosen number of milliseconds elapsed.

section: What if there is no object?
text:
What if there is no object?




The same program with an empty claw. The requested target stays at 130°. Ask what stalled() will report when the motor settles slightly beyond that target.
The actual motor angle settles at 132°, above the requested 130°. There is no object blocking the jaws, so stalled() remains False and the loop keeps checking. Draw attention to both readings: the movement can finish with a small position error. An exact check such as claw.angle() == GRIP_TARGET would also keep waiting on this settled reading.
Reveal claw.done(): it reports that the commanded movement has completed. Pybricks uses both position and speed tolerances to decide completion. This illustrative preset has a +2° settled error within a 3° position tolerance. The motor has stopped before done() becomes True. Merely passing the requested angle while still moving does not prove completion. The preset illustrates tolerances without simulating a real controller, and these numbers are not universal Pybricks defaults.
With both checks, the loop ends on done() in this empty trial and still ends on stalled() when an object blocks the jaws. Ask the last question: the loop ended, so is an object held? Here done() is True at 132° for a 130° request, with nothing between the jaws. Completion alone does not confirm a catch.
References: https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html#pybricks.pupdevices.Motor.done and https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html#pybricks.pupdevices.Motor.control.target_tolerances

Work through each row. Only False/False continues, which is exactly the two trials just run: the blocked object left on row two, the empty claw on row three. This table explains the Boolean expression; it does not claim all four combinations necessarily occur in this model.

section: What will an opening command change?
text:
What will an opening command change?




The object is held after the checking loop: the jaws are at 70°, the closing command is still active, and the effort limit is 180 mNm. Read the displayed command aloud and take predictions before running it.
The jaws open to 0° and the object is free. Point out that the opening command replaced the closing task; nothing had to cancel the earlier instruction first.
This sequence is release(). It has the same shape as the closing sequence: choose the effort limit, then run to a target. Default waiting is right here, because the next mission action follows arrival. Stage 11 asks how far it should actually open.

The three functions



home()

def home():
    claw.control.limits(
        torque=HOME_TORQUE)
    claw.run_until_stalled(
        -CLOSE_SPEED,
        then=Stop.COAST)
    wait(200)
    claw.reset_angle(0)
    claw.control.limits(
        torque=GRIP_TORQUE)

The built-in operation ends, then coasts.




grab()

def grab():
    claw.control.limits(
        torque=GRIP_TORQUE)
    claw.run_target(
        CLOSE_SPEED, GRIP_TARGET,
        then=Stop.HOLD,
        wait=False)
    wait(100)
    while (not claw.stalled()
           and not claw.done()):
        wait(10)

Our loop ends. The closing task stays active.




release()

def release(angle=OPEN_TARGET):
    claw.control.limits(
        torque=GRIP_TORQUE)
    claw.run_target(
        OPEN_SPEED, angle,
        then=Stop.COAST)

The opening reaches its target, then coasts.




Package everything the class has built. Reveal the three in order and read what ends each one, which is the line under each function.
home() and release() both wait for their own movement to finish. grab() cannot, because the movement it starts may never reach its target, so it starts the command with wait=False and watches for either outcome.
That difference has a consequence worth saying aloud: leaving our checking loop does not cancel the motor instruction. The closing command is still active while grab() returns, which is what keeps the object squeezed, and then=Stop.HOLD is what maintains the position if the target is actually reached. Demonstration prints and observation waits stay outside the functions. A return means one of the two conditions occurred; it does not certify a catch. This ends the excerpt covering stages 7-10.
